systems.name: Foundations of History Taking
systems.intro: The reasoning behind history taking itself — the shape of every consultation, the tool for dissecting any symptom, and the risk screen that meets the patient as a person. Master these three and every organ-system screen slots into place.

sections.name: The Clinical History — Structure
sections.scaffold: GREET → COMPLAINT → HPI → PAST → DRUGS → FAMILY → SOCIAL → REVIEW → ICE
sections.scaffoldIntro: Every history — no matter the presenting problem — hangs on the same skeleton. Learn the skeleton once and you can rebuild any history under pressure, then flex the detail to fit the patient. The order below is Talley’s: let the patient tell the story first (open), then take control and fill the gaps (directed).

chunks.mid: Rapport, then the story in the patient’s words
chunks.gen: Introduce & consent; open question; the "golden minute"; "What else?"

chunks.mid: The principal symptom that brought them in
chunks.gen: What concerns you most? (patient’s own words, no jargon)
Dose, duration, indication, adherence; OTC & complementary
Similar illness in relatives; ages/causes of death

chunks.mid: The person, their risks and supports
chunks.gen: Smoking, alcohol, drugs, occupation, home (see Social entry)

chunks.mid: Screen the other systems for missed disease
chunks.gen: Pertinent positives AND negatives (see the 13 system screens)

chunks.mid: The patient’s perspective and the effect of illness
chunks.gen: Ideas, Concerns, Expectations; "Is there anything else?"

sections.scaffoldOutro: Note the two halves: the patient leads the **first** half (open question, uninterrupted story — the average doctor interrupts inside ~20 seconds; give it closer to a minute), and the clinician leads the **second** half (specific questions to test hypotheses). Record the presenting complaint in the patient’s own words.

questions.ask: Introduce yourself and your role, gain consent, then: "What has been the trouble recently?" or "When were you last quite well?"
questions.why: Rapport is the substrate of an accurate history — patients disclose more when at ease. Open the interview with an open-ended question and then listen: as Osler put it, the patient will "tell you the diagnosis" if you let them. Avoid "What brought you in?" (invites "an ambulance").
points: Let the patient talk uninterrupted first → the "golden minute"; premature closure is the commonest interviewing error
"Is there anything else?" / "What else?" → reopens the story and surfaces the symptom they were building up to
Deep personal/social questions up front → can feel intrusive; defer until you’ve shown interest in the presenting problem

questions.ask: Of all these, which problem is troubling you the most?
questions.why: A patient often has several symptoms; you must decide which one led them to present — and the patient’s idea of "serious" may differ from yours (the person with a cold who mentions, in passing, coughing up blood needs attention on the chest, not the nose). Record it in the patient’s own words, no technical terms yet.
points: The symptom that most concerns the patient → must be addressed, even if minor, or they leave dissatisfied
A symptom mentioned "in passing" (e.g. haemoptysis) → may be the most important — don’t let the loudest complaint bury it

questions.ask: Tell me about it from the very beginning — when did you last feel completely well?
questions.why: The core of the history. Get the story in chronological order, one problem at a time. Characterise each symptom with SOCRATES, and frame every complaint against the four diagnostic questions: Where (anatomical), What (pathological), How (functional), Why (aetiological) — a diagnosis is a disease process, not just a name.
points: Where is it? → anatomical diagnosis · What is its nature? → pathological diagnosis
How does it affect you? → functional diagnosis · Why did it develop? → aetiological diagnosis
Finish one symptom before moving to the next → politely hold the garrulous patient: "I’d like to finish about your blackouts before we discuss the tiredness."

questions.ask: Have you had any serious illnesses, operations, or hospital admissions? Any childhood illnesses? Are your vaccinations up to date?
questions.why: Past illness shapes current risk and constrains investigation. Preface it ("These may affect your current tests and treatment") as it can feel intrusive. Some operations carry continuing risk (valve surgery, cancer surgery, prostheses); some conditions contraindicate tests.
points: Prostheses / pacemakers → pacemaker = MRI contraindication; foreign body = infection risk
CKD → caution with iodinated contrast and gadolinium; pregnancy → avoid radiation
A "diagnosis" the patient reports → verify it (untested "ulcer" may never have been one); keep objective scepticism

questions.ask: What tablets, inhalers, patches or medicines are you on — can you show me them all? Do you take anything from the chemist or any natural remedies? Any allergies?
questions.why: The drug list is a map of hidden diagnoses (an antihypertensive reveals forgotten "normal" blood pressure). Ask by drug class to jog memory, and about OTC/complementary agents (~50% use them; some adulterated). Aspirin/NSAIDs — but not paracetamol — cause GI bleeding.
points: Prompt by class → BP, cholesterol, diabetes, arthritis, mood, contraception (many don’t count "the pill"), HRT, epilepsy, anticoagulation
Capture dose, duration, indication, adherence, side effects for each
questions.red: always separate a TRUE allergy (rash, bronchospasm) from a side effect — patients routinely confuse them, and a mislabelled "allergy" narrows future treatment unnecessarily. Ask exactly what the reaction was.

questions.ask: Do any illnesses run in your family? Are your parents and siblings well — if not, what did they have, and at what age?
questions.why: Familial clustering flags both inherited disease and shared risk. Premature IHD in a first-degree relative is a major risk factor; bowel and breast cancer are the two malignancies patients report accurately. Draw a family tree if a heritable disorder is suspected.
points: Numerous affected relatives, earlier-than-usual onset, the less-often-affected sex, or disease despite no risk factors → raised genetic risk
Consanguinity → increases autosomal-recessive risk — ask tactfully if the pedigree suggests it

questions.ask: A quick run through the other systems — have you had any [targeted screen of head-to-toe symptoms]?
questions.why: The safety net: a brief screen of the systems you haven’t covered, to catch important disease the presenting complaint would otherwise miss. Experienced clinicians do a TARGETED review guided by what they’ve already heard — not every question on every patient.
points: Record pertinent NEGATIVES, not just positives → they narrow the differential and document your reasoning
A new symptom unmasked here → stop and characterise it fully, then fold it back into the HPI

questions.ask: What do you think might be going on? Is there anything you’re particularly worried about? What were you hoping we could do? — and how has this affected your life?
questions.why: Before closing, elicit the patient’s Ideas, Concerns and Expectations, and the illness’s functional/psychological impact. Their chief worry may not be the worst symptom but a specific fear — addressing it is central to rapport and to a management plan they’ll follow.
points: Ask what they think is wrong and most fear → often reframes the consultation entirely
A serious illness reshapes work, finances, relationships and self-esteem → ask how they’re coping and what they hope for

items: Chronological, one problem at a time

discriminator.title: the four diagnostic questions (what every complaint should answer)
rows: Stops you walking to the letterbox → severity & disability
Smoker, diabetic, family history → coronary risk

sections.clnote: Osler’s rule anchors the whole method: "the patient tells you the diagnosis — you just have to listen and ask the right questions." The history is the cheapest and highest-yield diagnostic test you own; exam and investigations mostly confirm what a good history already suggested.

sections.name: SOCRATES — Analysing Any Symptom
sections.scaffold: S ite · O nset · C haracter · R adiation · A ssociated · T iming · E xacerbating/relieving · S everity
sections.scaffoldIntro: SOCRATES is the tool that turns a vague complaint into a characterised symptom you can reason about. It works for ANY symptom (not just pain) — Radiation is the one element reserved for pain or discomfort. Run every presenting symptom through it in the HPI.

chunks.gen: "Point to exactly where." Localised vs diffuse
Sudden vs gradual; what were you doing at the time?
Does it move or spread anywhere?
Symptoms of the same system — the combination diagnoses
When did it start? Constant vs intermittent? Why present now?
What makes it better or worse?
Does it stop you doing things? Graded mild→very severe

sections.scaffoldOutro: The power is in the pattern, not any single answer: it is usually the COMBINATION of characteristic features — not one symptom — that reliably suggests the diagnosis. Onset and the exacerbating/relieving pair are often the most discriminating letters.

questions.ask: Where exactly is it? Can you point to the spot?
questions.why: Localisation narrows the anatomy. Ask the patient to point — and note that some symptoms deliberately don’t localise (dizziness, cough, breathlessness, weight change), which is itself informative.
points: Well-localised, patient points with one finger → somatic/parietal source (e.g. localised peritonitis)
Diffuse, can’t pinpoint → visceral or non-localised symptom (early appendicitis is vague periumbilical before it localises)

questions.ask: How did it start — suddenly or gradually? What were you doing at that moment?
questions.why: Mode of onset is one of the most discriminating questions in medicine. Instantaneous onset and offset points to arrhythmia; a sudden severe "thunderclap" points to a catastrophe; what the patient was doing at onset can hand you the diagnosis.
points: Instantaneous on AND off → cardiac arrhythmia
Breathlessness that WAKES them from sleep → cardiac failure (PND)
Sudden loss of consciousness with immediate full recovery → cardiac (arrhythmia), not neurological
questions.red: a sudden, severe "worst-ever" headache reaching peak in seconds (thunderclap) → subarachnoid haemorrhage until proven otherwise.

questions.ask: What is it actually like? If you had to describe the feeling…
questions.why: Force the patient to define the symptom in their own terms, because lay words hide different meanings. "Dizziness" may be vertigo (room spinning) or presyncope; "indigestion" may mean pain, heartburn, fullness, wind or altered bowel habit. Pin it down: "What do you mean by …?"
points: Vertigo (room spins) → vestibular/neurological; light-headed "about to faint" → presyncope/cardiovascular
Chest pain described as "sharp" → makes angina LESS likely (ischaemic pain is typically heavy/tight/dull)

questions.ask: Does the pain travel or spread anywhere else?
questions.why: Applies mainly to pain. Certain radiation patterns are characteristic or even diagnostic — the pattern of spread points to the source or the nerve territory involved.
points: Pain in a dermatomal (nerve-root) band → e.g. herpes zoster / radiculopathy
Central chest pain radiating to jaw or arm → supports cardiac ischaemia; to the back, tearing → dissection

questions.ask: Have you noticed anything else that comes with it?
questions.why: Systematically uncover the symptoms expected with disease of that region — give first and fullest attention to the system of the presenting complaint. A single symptom may be the clue, but the characteristic CLUSTER is what reliably makes the diagnosis.
points: Chest pain + sweating + nausea + breathlessness → the ischaemic cluster
Headache + fever + neck stiffness + photophobia → the meningitic cluster

questions.ask: When did it first begin? Is it there all the time or does it come and go? Why have you come about it now?
questions.why: Date the onset as precisely as you can — "what was the first thing you noticed was wrong?" and "when did you last feel entirely well?" Establish continuous vs intermittent, and in long-standing symptoms ask why they’re presenting today (a change usually prompts it).
points: Intermittent, stereotyped, fully resolves between → paroxysmal process (arrhythmia, migraine, TIA)
Progressive, never fully clears → structural/chronic process
Ask about prior similar episodes → recurrence pattern is diagnostic in itself

questions.ask: Does anything make it better or worse?
questions.why: Modifiers are frequently the most specific clue to mechanism. What relieves or provokes a symptom often localises the organ and the pathology.
points: Relieved by sitting forward → pericarditis; relieved by antacid/milk → acid reflux
Worse on the slightest movement → peritonitis; worse on movement/weight-bearing in the big toe → gout
Brought on by exertion, relieved by rest → angina (or claudication in the legs)

questions.ask: How bad is it — does it stop you doing things, or wake you from sleep?
questions.why: Severity is subjective; the best anchor is FUNCTIONAL impact, not a bare number. Grade mild (ignorable) → moderate (can’t be ignored) → severe (limits daily activity) → very severe. Quantify concretely where you can (metres walked before breathless; rest vs exertional angina).
points: Grade by interference with activity/sleep → more reproducible than "out of 10"
Concrete quantification → SOB after 10 m on the flat is worse than after 90 m uphill; angina at rest is more significant than on exertion
The 0–10 scale is better for tracking change over time than absolute severity — and demanding a number from someone in severe pain can be unkind

checklist: Site — where exactly; localised vs diffuse
Onset — sudden vs gradual; activity at onset
Character — what the symptom actually is ("what do you mean by…?")
Timing — onset date, constant vs intermittent, why now

discriminator.title: onset & pattern — what the mode of onset signals
rows: Electrical events start and stop abruptly

sections.clnote: SOCRATES works for any symptom — Radiation is the only pain-specific letter. Reach first for Onset and the Exacerbating/relieving pair: they are usually the most discriminating, and the diagnosis lives in the COMBINATION of features, not one answer.

sections.name: Social History & Risk Screen
sections.scaffold: HOME → OCCUPATION → SMOKING → ALCOHOL → DRUGS → LIFESTYLE → MOOD & INTIMACY
sections.scaffoldIntro: The social history is where you meet the patient as a person — and where much of the modifiable risk and the discharge-planning reality lives. Ask it conversationally, not as a rote checklist. It carries the highest-yield named screening tools (WHACS, pack-years, CAGE/AUDIT-C, the single-question drug screen).

chunks.gen: Who’s at home? Managing? Caregiver? Steps/toilet? Driving?
WHACS: What / How / Anything concerning / Colleagues / Satisfied
Ever smoked? How many/day × how many years → pack-years
Type, how much, how often; CAGE / AUDIT-C
Single-question screen; IV use & needle sharing
Diet adequacy, activity level, recent overseas travel
Mood/anhedonia screen; sexual history if relevant

sections.scaffoldOutro: Match depth to relevance and timing: living situation and function matter most in chronic/disabling illness; the intrusive questions (sexual history, drug use, mood) land better once rapport is built — sometimes at a later consultation. Use the social history as the natural moment for smoking-cessation and safe-drinking advice.

questions.ask: Who’s at home with you? Are you managing day to day on your own? How do you get to the shops?
questions.why: Determines whether the person can safely function — the pivot of any discharge or management plan in chronic or disabling illness. Establish the main caregiver, the physical setup (steps to the door, location of the toilet), and mobility.
points: Can’t manage ADLs unaided → identify the main caregiver and available social support early
Physical barriers (steps, upstairs toilet) → shape rehab and discharge planning

questions.ask: What do you do for work? What does that involve day to day? — (WHACS)
questions.why: Occupation and hobbies link directly to disease. The WHACS mnemonic structures it: What do you do? How do you do it? Anything you’re concerned about (exposures)? Colleagues affected? Satisfied with the job? Ask specifically about dusts, chemicals and biological exposures.
points: Dust/mineral exposure → asbestosis (builders, shipyards), silicosis (stonemasons, miners), pneumoconiosis (coal)
Organic/biological exposure → hypersensitivity pneumonitis (farmers’ mouldy hay, bird fanciers), occupational asthma (timber)
Ask if fellow workers are affected → shared exposure supports an occupational cause

questions.ask: Have you ever smoked? How many a day, and for how many years? Have you stopped — when? Do you vape?
questions.why: Never ask only "do you smoke?" (a patient who quit this morning says no). Quantify as PACK-YEARS — (cigarettes/day ÷ 20) × years — because risk scales with cumulative dose and recency. Ask about vaping separately (nicotine content, EVALI risk).
points: 1 pack-year = 20 cigarettes/day for 1 year → the standard unit of tobacco burden
Smoking → premature coronary & peripheral vascular disease, COPD, many cancers, peptic ulcer, fetal harm
Modern packs hold 30–50, not 20 → clarify actual number to compute pack-years correctly

questions.ask: Do you drink alcohol? Beer, wine or spirits — and how many glasses on most days? — then screen (CAGE / AUDIT-C).
questions.why: Quantify first (1 standard drink ≈ 8–10 g ethanol), then screen for a use disorder. Self-report is often an underestimate — hold it with gentle scepticism. Liver risk rises above ~80 g/day (men) or ~40 g/day (women) sustained for years.
points: CAGE ≥ 2 "yes" → suggests dependence (Cut down / Annoyed / Guilty / Eye-opener; 77% sens, 79% spec)
AUDIT-C ≥ 3 (women) / ≥ 4 (men) → unhealthy use — more sensitive than CAGE for excess drinking short of dependence
Excess alcohol → look for its complications: liver disease, pancreatitis, GI bleeding, cardiomyopathy/AF, withdrawal, neuropathy
questions.red: flag the guideline nuance: Talley gives BOTH CAGE and AUDIT-C but notes CAGE misses unhealthy drinking short of dependence, so AUDIT-C (or the single "how many times in the past year 5+/4+ drinks?" question) is preferred for screening. Current NHMRC (AU) safe limits: ≤ 10 standard drinks/week AND ≤ 4 on any one day.

questions.ask: How many times in the past year have you used a recreational drug, or a prescription medication for non-medical reasons?
questions.why: That single question is ~100% sensitive (74% specific) for problem drug use — an efficient, non-judgemental opener. Injecting use adds blood-borne-virus and endocarditis risk; ask about needle sharing.
points: Any non-zero answer → explore substances, route, frequency, and dependence
IV use → HIV/hepatitis B & C, right-sided endocarditis, injection-site infection; ask about needle sharing
Judge relevance — no need to interrogate the 90-year-old nursing-home resident

questions.ask: Tell me briefly about your diet and how physically active you are. Have you travelled overseas recently?
questions.why: Lifestyle modifies cardiometabolic risk; travel reframes infection risk. For diet, note adequacy and who cooks (frailty/social clue). For travel, ask destinations, how they lived (water, food), any illness or hospitalisation abroad, and malaria prophylaxis.
points: Recent travel + fever → ask destination, exposures, prophylaxis (malaria), and overseas hospitalisation (resistant organisms)
Poor diet / can’t cook / relies on others → nutritional and functional red flag in the frail or elderly

questions.ask: How are things going at home and at work? Have you been feeling down, or lost interest in things you normally enjoy? — and, where relevant, a sexual history.
questions.why: Depression is common (prevalence up to ~8%) and increases threefold with any significant medical illness — screen with mood + anhedonia; a "no" to both makes major depression unlikely. The sexual history is asked only when relevant and with good timing (see Reproductive).
points: Low mood AND anhedonia → screen further; if depression likely, ask about suicidal ideation (asking does NOT increase risk)
Organic mimics of depression → hypothyroidism, Cushing’s — keep them in mind
Defer intrusive sexual/personal questions until rapport is established — good judgement on timing matters

sections.drill: **HOME:** who’s home, support, ADLs, caregiver, access/driving · **OCCUPATION:** WHACS + specific exposures (dust/chemical/biological) · **SMOKING:** pack-years (/day÷20×years) + vaping · **ALCOHOL:** quantify (std drinks) + CAGE/AUDIT-C + NHMRC ≤10/wk, ≤4/day · **DRUGS:** single-question screen; IV → BBV/endocarditis · **LIFESTYLE:** diet, exercise, travel (+ prophylaxis) · **MOOD & INTIMACY:** mood + anhedonia (± suicide risk), sexual history if relevant

Current NHMRC (AU) safe drinking: ≤ 10 standard drinks/week AND ≤ 4 on any single day. See verification-report.md §C.

systems.name: General / Constitutional
systems.scaffoldIntro: The constitutional screen is the body's "check engine light" — non-specific signals that something systemic (malignancy, infection, inflammation, endocrine) is going on. Group them by what they signal:
systems.scaffoldOutro: This is the screen that catches the "must-not-miss" systemic diseases the organ-specific screens can miss. The **B-symptom triad** (weight loss + fever + drenching night sweats) lives here and is one of the highest-yield clusters in the systems review — it flags lymphoma and TB.

questions.ask: Has your weight changed recently without trying? Are your clothes looser?
questions.why: Unintentional weight loss is one of the most important symptoms in medicine. Quantify it (kilograms, timeframe) and confirm it's unintentional. >5% body weight over 6–12 months is significant.
points: Unintentional weight loss + good/increased appetite → hypermetabolic: hyperthyroidism, or uncontrolled diabetes (osmotic loss)
Unintentional weight loss + poor appetite → malignancy, chronic infection (TB, HIV), depression, chronic organ failure
Weight gain → fluid (cardiac/renal/liver failure), hypothyroidism, Cushing's, or simple positive energy balance
Rapid weight gain over days → fluid retention, not fat
questions.red: unexplained weight loss is a cancer red flag at any age — pair it with the sinister screens of every organ system.

questions.ask: Any fevers or shivering attacks? Drenching night sweats where you change the sheets?
questions.why: Fever signals infection/inflammation/malignancy. **Rigors** (uncontrollable shaking) suggest bacteraemia. **Drenching** night sweats flag TB, lymphoma, and endocarditis.
points: Rigors + localising symptoms → bacterial infection (pyelonephritis, cholangitis, pneumonia, abscess)
Drenching night sweats + weight loss + lumps → lymphoma; + cough/travel → TB
Recurrent fevers with a heart murmur / IVDU / dental work → endocarditis
Cyclical fevers with travel to endemic area → malaria

questions.ask: How is your energy overall? Do you feel generally run down?
questions.why: The most common and least specific symptom — its value is contextual. Screen for the treatable drivers rather than accepting "tired" at face value.
points: Fatigue + cold intolerance + weight gain + constipation → hypothyroidism
Fatigue + low mood + anhedonia + sleep/appetite change → depression
Always ask about sleep quantity and quality and medications (beta-blockers, sedatives) before attributing to disease

questions.ask: How is your appetite? Are you eating normally?
questions.why: Appetite links the constitutional screen to GI, endocrine and psychiatric systems, and modifies the interpretation of weight change (see above).

questions.ask: Any lumps in the neck, armpits or groin? Any generalised itching?
questions.why: Lymphadenopathy is the physical correlate of the lymphoreticular malignancies and chronic infections. Generalised **pruritus without a rash** is a classic paraneoplastic/systemic clue.
points: Rubbery, painless, persistent nodes ± B symptoms → lymphoma
Tender nodes with local infection → reactive
Generalised itch without rash → lymphoma (esp. Hodgkin), cholestasis, iron deficiency, chronic kidney disease, polycythaemia, thyroid disease

systems.drill: **WASTING:** weight change (quantified, intentional?) · **THERMOSTAT:** fever, rigors, night sweats · **ENERGY:** fatigue, malaise, sleep · **APPETITE:** appetite/intake · **LUMPS:** lumps/lymphadenopathy, generalised itch
systems.clnote: B-symptom triad — weight loss + fever + drenching night sweats — is one of the highest-yield clusters in the whole review (think lymphoma, TB).

systems.name: Cardiovascular
systems.scaffoldIntro: Think of the heart's jobs failing one at a time, moving outward from the chest:

chunks.gen: Dyspnoea, orthopnoea, PND, ankle swelling, fatigue

chunks.mid: The substrate for all of the above
chunks.gen: HTN, diabetes, lipids, smoking, family history, rheumatic fever

systems.scaffoldOutro: If you can say "pain, pump, rhythm, vessels, risk" you can rebuild all ~10 questions from first principles. The pump chunk has an internal logic too: congestion behind the left heart shows up in the lungs (dyspnoea → orthopnoea → PND, in order of severity), congestion behind the right heart shows up in the legs (oedema).

questions.ask: Have you had any pain, tightness or discomfort in your chest?
questions.why: Chest pain is the cardinal symptom of myocardial ischaemia, but the character is what discriminates between the life-threats (ACS, dissection, PE, tension pneumothorax) and the benign mimics (MSK, GORD, anxiety). Always characterise fully with SOCRATES (Site, Onset, Character, Radiation, Associated symptoms, Timing, Exacerbating/relieving factors, Severity).
points: Central, crushing/tight, radiating to jaw/left arm, on exertion, relieved by rest → rules in angina (note: GTN relief alone is not specific — it also relieves oesophageal spasm and carries a placebo effect); if at rest >30 min with sweating/nausea → ACS
Tearing pain radiating to the back, abrupt maximal onset → aortic dissection until proven otherwise
Sharp, worse on inspiration → shifts you towards pleuritic causes (PE, pericarditis, pneumothorax) — note pericarditis pain classically eases sitting forward
Worse on palpation or specific movement → MSK, but never rule out ACS on this alone
Burning, related to meals/lying flat, relieved by antacids → GORD
questions.red: rest pain, crescendo pattern (unstable angina), associated syncope or diaphoresis, tearing interscapular pain.

followups.q: Can you describe the pain — sharp or dull, heavy or tight?
followups.probes: Character does most of the work: tight/heavy/crushing → ischaemic pattern · sharp/stabbing → pleuritic or pericardial · burning → reflux

followups.q: When do you get it — out of the blue, or with exertion? Worse after a meal or in the cold?
followups.probes: Exertional, reproducible → angina · unrelated to exertion, worse lying down or after meals → reflux

followups.q: How long does it last, and does it ease with rest?
followups.probes: Minutes, eases with rest → stable angina · over 30 min at rest, unrelieved → acute coronary syndrome

followups.q: Does it radiate anywhere — jaw, arms, back?
followups.probes: Radiation to jaw/left arm → cardiac · sudden tearing pain radiating to the back → aortic dissection

followups.q: Is it coming on with less effort than before, or now at rest?
followups.probes: A crescendo pattern or pain at rest → unstable angina/ACS, needs urgent assessment

followups.q: Any sweating, nausea, or feeling faint with it?
followups.probes: Sweating, nausea and breathlessness alongside the pain raise the likelihood of ACS

followups.q: Is it affected by breathing, movement, or position?
followups.probes: Worse on inspiration → pleuritic (PE, pericarditis, pneumothorax); worse on movement/palpation → musculoskeletal — but never rule out ACS on this alone

followups.q: Have you taken anything for it — does a spray under the tongue, or an antacid, help?
followups.probes: GTN relief is not specific — it also eases oesophageal spasm and carries a placebo effect — so use it to support, not confirm, an ischaemic cause

questions.ask: Do you get short of breath? How far can you walk on the flat before stopping?
questions.why: Exertional dyspnoea is the earliest symptom of left ventricular failure — pulmonary congestion raises the work of breathing before any signs appear. Quantifying exercise tolerance (metres on the flat, flights of stairs) gives you a severity yardstick (NYHA class) and a baseline to track change: "what could you do a year ago vs now?"
points: Gradual decline in exercise tolerance + orthopnoea/PND/oedema → rules in cardiac failure
Dyspnoea with wheeze, cough, sputum, smoking history → shifts towards respiratory (COPD/asthma) — this is the great cardio-resp discriminator zone; see the table at the end
Sudden-onset dyspnoea → think PE, pneumothorax, flash pulmonary oedema, arrhythmia
Dyspnoea on exertion with exertional chest tightness → may be an angina equivalent, especially in diabetics and the elderly
questions.red: dyspnoea at rest, rapidly progressive over days.

followups.q: How far can you walk on the flat, or how many stairs, before you're stopped? Compared with a year ago?
followups.probes: Quantify — this maps onto NYHA class and gives a trajectory, more reliable than the patient's own severity grading

followups.q: Did it come on suddenly, or has it crept up gradually?
followups.probes: Sudden → MI, pulmonary oedema, arrhythmia, PE · gradual → progressive left ventricular impairment

followups.q: Any tightness in the chest when you're breathless?
followups.probes: Dyspnoea with exertional chest tightness may be an angina equivalent, especially in diabetics and the elderly

followups.q: Do you get breathless lying flat, or wake at night gasping?
followups.probes: Orthopnoea/PND strongly favour a cardiac over a respiratory cause — pursue with those specific questions

followups.q: Any wheeze, cough, sputum, or a smoking history?
followups.probes: Pulls the picture toward a respiratory cause (COPD/asthma) rather than cardiac — the classic cardio-resp discriminator zone

followups.q: Any past heart attacks, angina, high blood pressure, or heavy alcohol use?
followups.probes: Known IHD points to reduced LV contractility; hypertension or heavy alcohol intake point to hypertensive heart disease or alcoholic cardiomyopathy

followups.q: Does it feel like you can't get a big enough breath in, coming on at rest rather than with exertion?
followups.probes: Suggests anxiety-related breathlessness — a diagnosis of exclusion, not the first assumption

questions.ask: How many pillows do you sleep with? What happens if you lie flat?
questions.why: Lying flat returns pooled venous blood from the legs to the chest. A failing left ventricle can't handle the extra preload, so pulmonary congestion worsens within minutes of lying down. The pillow count is a semi-quantitative severity score.
points: Breathlessness within minutes of lying flat, relieved by sitting up → strongly favours LVF over lung disease as the cause of dyspnoea
COPD patients may also prefer sitting up, but their limitation is all-day and effort-related rather than positional — ask "is it lying flat itself that makes you breathless?"
New increase in pillow count → decompensation

followups.q: How many pillows do you use, and has that changed recently?
followups.probes: Pillow count is a semi-quantitative severity score — a new increase signals decompensation

followups.q: Is it lying flat itself that brings it on, or are you just generally limited by effort?
followups.probes: True orthopnoea is positional and rapid (minutes) — COPD patients may also prefer sitting up, but their limitation is effort-related and all-day, not positional

followups.q: How quickly does it come on after lying down, and does sitting up relieve it?
followups.probes: Onset within minutes of lying flat, relieved by sitting up, strongly favours LVF over lung disease as the cause of dyspnoea

questions.ask: Do you ever wake at night gasping for air and need to sit up or go to the window?
questions.why: During sleep, gradual reabsorption of interstitial fluid and nocturnal reduction in adrenergic drive let pulmonary oedema accumulate; the patient wakes 1–2 hours in, suffocating, and must sit or stand for several minutes to recover. It is one of the more specific congestion symptoms for left heart failure (Talley quantifies only orthopnoea, which strongly favours LVF over lung disease).
points: Classic story (waking gasping, relieved slowly by sitting/standing) → rules in LVF with high specificity
Distinguish from nocturnal asthma (wheeze-predominant, often with cough, responds to inhaler) and OSA (witnessed apnoeas, snoring, unrefreshed sleep — the patient's partner often gives the history)
questions.red: new PND = decompensated heart failure until proven otherwise.

followups.q: How long after falling asleep does it happen, and what do you have to do to recover — sit up, stand, go to the window?
followups.probes: Waking 1–2 hours in, gasping, needing several minutes upright to recover, is the classic pattern — highly specific for LVF

followups.q: Is it wheeze that wakes you, and does an inhaler help?
followups.probes: Wheeze-predominant, with cough, responsive to an inhaler, points to nocturnal asthma instead

followups.q: Does your partner notice loud snoring or pauses in your breathing?
followups.probes: Witnessed apnoeas/snoring with unrefreshed sleep points to OSA rather than PND

followups.q: Is this new, or has it happened before?
followups.probes: New PND = decompensated heart failure until proven otherwise

questions.ask: Any swelling of the ankles or legs? Worse through the day?
questions.why: Right heart congestion raises venous pressure, pushing fluid into dependent tissue. Gravity makes it worst in the evening and after standing.
points: Bilateral, pitting, worse by evening, with other failure symptoms → rules in congestive cardiac failure
Unilateral swelling → think DVT or local cause (cellulitis, ruptured Baker's cyst) — a completely different pathway
Bilateral oedema without dyspnoea → consider hypoalbuminaemia (nephrotic, liver disease), calcium-channel blockers (amlodipine is a classic), venous insufficiency, or pelvic obstruction
Ask about abdominal swelling and weight gain — ascites and rapid weight gain suggest significant fluid retention

followups.q: Is it both ankles, or just one?
followups.probes: Bilateral → systemic/cardiac cause · unilateral → DVT or a local cause (cellulitis, ruptured Baker's cyst) — a completely different pathway

followups.q: Worse by evening, better after a night lying flat?
followups.probes: The classic pattern of dependent, cardiac-origin oedema

followups.q: Any breathlessness, orthopnoea or PND alongside it?
followups.probes: Oedema plus the pump-failure cluster rules in congestive cardiac failure — oedema alone is poorly correlated with heart failure

followups.q: Any recent weight gain, or swelling of the abdomen?
followups.probes: Rapid weight gain (3 kg or more) and ascites suggest significant fluid retention

followups.q: Any new medications, especially for blood pressure?
followups.probes: Calcium-channel blockers (e.g. amlodipine) are a classic drug cause of peripheral oedema unrelated to the heart

questions.ask: How is your energy? More tired than you used to be?
questions.why: Low cardiac output presents as fatigue before frank dyspnoea in some patients (especially the elderly). Non-specific alone — its value is in aggregate with the pump-failure cluster. Also a common symptom of beta-blocker therapy — review the medication list.
points: Fatigue accompanying dyspnoea, orthopnoea, PND or oedema → part of the low-output/congestive picture, and may precede frank breathlessness, especially in the elderly
Fatigue in isolation, or explained by poor sleep, anaemia, depression or a new beta-blocker → look outside cardiac failure first

followups.q: Is this fatigue different from feeling normal tiredness — is it limiting what you can do?
followups.probes: Low-output fatigue tracks with exertion and may precede frank dyspnoea, especially in the elderly

followups.q: Any breathlessness, ankle swelling, or chest symptoms alongside it?
followups.probes: Fatigue is non-specific alone — its value is in aggregate with the pump-failure cluster

followups.q: Are you on a beta-blocker, or any new medication?
followups.probes: Beta-blockers commonly cause fatigue — review the medication list before assuming cardiac decompensation

followups.q: Any other explanation — poor sleep, low mood, or heavy periods/bleeding?
followups.probes: Rules out the other common causes of fatigue — anaemia, depression, poor sleep — before anchoring on cardiac output

questions.ask: Are you ever aware of your heart racing, thumping or skipping? Can you tap out the rhythm?
questions.why: "Palpitations" means ten different things to ten patients. The tapped rhythm, mode of onset/offset, and company the symptom keeps let you separate benign ectopics from dangerous arrhythmias.
points: Fast, irregularly irregular → AF — ask about precipitants (alcohol, caffeine, thyroid symptoms) and stroke risk factors
Abrupt on/off, regular, fast; may terminate with vagal manoeuvres → SVT
Occasional "missed beat then a thump" at rest, disappearing on exercise → benign ectopics
Gradual onset with anxiety, hyperventilation, tingling → panic attack — but exclude arrhythmia first, not the other way round
Palpitations with syncope or chest pain → possible VT / structural disease
questions.red: palpitations + syncope, family history of sudden death (channelopathies, HOCM), known structural heart disease.

followups.q: Can you tap out the rhythm for me — is it fast or slow, regular or irregular?
followups.probes: The tapped rhythm is often more useful than the verbal description — irregularly irregular → AF · very fast and regular → SVT/VT

followups.q: How does it start and stop — suddenly, or does it build up gradually?
followups.probes: Abrupt on/off → arrhythmia (SVT/VT) · gradual → sinus tachycardia (anxiety, exertion, fever)

followups.q: How long do episodes last, and how often do they happen?
followups.probes: Brief and occasional suggests resting ectopics; sustained episodes need more urgent characterisation

followups.q: Any chest tightness or breathlessness with it?
followups.probes: Palpitations + chest tightness/dyspnoea raise concern for a haemodynamically significant arrhythmia

followups.q: Have you ever blacked out, or felt about to, during an episode?
followups.probes: Palpitations + syncope suggest VT, especially with known structural heart disease

followups.q: Any triggers — caffeine, alcohol, stress — or things that stop it, like holding your breath or coughing?
followups.probes: Response to vagal manoeuvres (Valsalva, cold water, coughing) supports SVT

followups.q: Has a smartwatch or home monitor recorded anything?
followups.probes: Increasingly common corroborating evidence, but these devices are often confused by ectopic beats — don't over-interpret an unreviewed alert

followups.q: Any family history of unexplained sudden death, or known heart disease yourself?
followups.probes: Raises concern for inherited channelopathies (long QT, Brugada) or structural disease underlying the arrhythmia

questions.ask: Have you ever blacked out or felt you were about to? What were you doing?
questions.why: Cardiac syncope (arrhythmia, outflow obstruction) kills; vasovagal syncope doesn't. The circumstances are almost the whole diagnosis.
points: Syncope during exertion → rules in sinister causes: aortic stenosis, HOCM, VT — never dismiss it
No warning, rapid full recovery → arrhythmic (Stokes–Adams); note injury is uncommon in cardiac syncope, so its absence does not reassure
Prodrome of nausea, sweating, greying vision, triggered by standing/pain/emotion, rapid recovery → vasovagal — rules out cardiac cause with reasonable confidence
On standing → orthostatic hypotension — review antihypertensives, diuretics, and ask about fluid losses

Lateral tongue-biting and post-ictal confusion/drowsiness → shifts to seizure, a different system entirely (jerk duration is not a reliable discriminator: brief clonic jerks occur in ordinary convulsive syncope, and prolonged jerking actually suggests non-epileptic seizures)
questions.red: exertional syncope, syncope with no prodrome, family history of sudden cardiac death.

followups.q: What were you doing right when it happened?
followups.probes: Circumstances are almost the whole diagnosis — exertional syncope is sinister (AS, HOCM, VT); standing, coughing or micturition point to reflex/situational causes

followups.q: Was there any warning — nausea, sweating, tunnel vision — or did it come out of nowhere?
followups.probes: A vasovagal prodrome rules out a cardiac cause with reasonable confidence; no warning at all suggests an arrhythmic (Stokes–Adams) cause

followups.q: How quickly did you recover, and were you confused or drowsy afterwards?
followups.probes: Rapid, full recovery favours cardiac/vasovagal; slow recovery with confusion favours seizure or a neurological cause

followups.q: Did you bite your tongue, or did anyone see jerking movements?
followups.probes: Lateral tongue-biting and prolonged jerking suggest seizure — though brief clonic jerks can occur in ordinary convulsive syncope, so don't over-weight jerking alone

followups.q: Any chest pain, palpitations, or known heart disease beforehand?
followups.probes: Suggests an arrhythmic or ischaemic cause, especially with a background of structural heart disease

followups.q: Did it happen on standing up, or after a meal or dehydration? Any recent change to your blood pressure tablets?
followups.probes: Points to orthostatic hypotension — review antihypertensives, diuretics and fluid losses

followups.q: Any family history of sudden unexplained death at a young age?
followups.probes: Raises concern for inherited channelopathies (long/short QT, Brugada syndrome)

followups.q: Has anyone filmed an episode, or do you wear a device that might have recorded it?
followups.probes: A bystander video or smartwatch ECG can be the single most useful piece of evidence you'll get

questions.ask: Do you get cramping calf or buttock pain on walking that eases with rest?
questions.why: The peripheral arteries share the same atherosclerotic disease as the coronaries — claudication marks the patient as a vasculopath (their biggest killer is MI, not the leg). Claudication distance is the severity yardstick.
points: Reproducible cramping at a fixed walking distance, relieved within minutes of standing still → rules in peripheral arterial disease
Pain relieved only by sitting/leaning forward (not just stopping) and associated with back pain → spinal claudication (canal stenosis)
Rest pain, worse at night, relieved by hanging the foot out of bed → critical limb ischaemia — red flag, needs urgent vascular review
Ask also about cold feet, colour change, ulcers that won't heal
questions.red: Rest pain / critical limb ischaemia needs urgent vascular review.

followups.q: Where do you feel it — calf, thigh, or buttock — and how far can you walk before it starts?
followups.probes: Location clues the level of arterial disease; claudication distance is the severity yardstick

followups.q: Does it ease within a few minutes of stopping, or do you need to sit down first?
followups.probes: Relief on simply standing still → vascular claudication · relief only on sitting/leaning forward, with back pain → spinal (pseudo-)claudication from canal stenosis

followups.q: Does the pain ever happen at rest, especially at night, and does hanging your foot out of bed help?
followups.probes: Rest pain relieved by dependency → critical limb ischaemia, needs urgent vascular review

followups.q: Any colour change, coldness, or sores/ulcers on your feet that won't heal?
followups.probes: Pallor, coldness and non-healing ulcers complete the peripheral arterial disease picture (the six Ps)

followups.q: Do you have diabetes, high blood pressure, or a smoking history?
followups.probes: The same atherosclerotic risk factors — this patient's biggest killer is MI, not the leg

questions.ask: High blood pressure, diabetes or cholesterol? Do you smoke? How's your weight and activity level?
questions.why: These set the pre-test probability for everything above and are the targets of secondary prevention.
points: Hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidaemia, smoking (quantify pack-years), obesity, physical inactivity → each independently raises atherosclerotic risk

questions.ask: Any heart disease in the family — particularly at a young age?
questions.why: A first-degree relative with premature IHD (male <55, female <65) raises the patient's own risk independent of their other risk factors.
points: First-degree relative, male <55 / female <65, with IHD → premature family history, a non-modifiable risk factor

questions.ask: Did you have rheumatic fever as a child?
questions.why: Rheumatic fever causes valvular disease that only declares itself decades later — still relevant in older patients and in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities, where rates remain high.
points: Rheumatic fever in childhood → valvular disease (esp. mitral) decades later

discriminator.title: is the dyspnoea cardiac or respiratory?
rows: Uncommon (COPD sits up for effort, not position)

systems.drill: PAIN: chest pain (SOCRATES) · PUMP: dyspnoea + exercise tolerance, orthopnoea, PND, ankle swelling, fatigue · RHYTHM: palpitations, syncope/presyncope · VESSELS: claudication, rest pain, cold feet · RISK: HTN, DM, lipids, smoking, FHx, rheumatic fever
systems.seeAlso: Respiratory — the cardiac-vs-respiratory dyspnoea split is shared between the two

systems.name: Respiratory
systems.scaffold: AIRWAY → AIR SACS → LINING → SINISTER → CONTEXT
systems.scaffoldIntro: Follow the air down the tract, then step outward through the anatomy, then zoom out to the sinister and the contextual:

chunks.mid: The exposures that cause lung disease
chunks.gen: Smoking, occupation, pets/travel, TB contact, snoring/OSA

systems.scaffoldOutro: The airway chunk flows logically: air moving through a diseased tube makes noise (wheeze), irritates it (cough), and the tube produces secretions (sputum). Say "airway, air sacs, lining, sinister, context" and the ~11 questions rebuild themselves.
systems.seeAlso: ENT & Eyes — epistaxis, hoarseness, sore throat and other URTI symptoms

questions.ask: Do you have a cough? How long has it lasted? Worse at any particular time?
questions.why: Duration and pattern do most of the diagnostic work. The single most important split is acute (<3 weeks) vs chronic (>8 weeks) — acute is usually infective; chronic demands an explanation.
points: Chronic productive cough, most days for 3 months in 2 consecutive years → rules in chronic bronchitis (COPD) by definition
Dry nocturnal cough, with wheeze, worse with exercise/cold air/allergens → asthma (nocturnal symptoms = poor control)
Dry cough on an ACE inhibitor → drug cause; check the medication list before ordering anything

Bovine (hollow, non-explosive) cough with hoarseness → recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy (vocal cords can't close); note a barking cough is croup/tracheomalacia and a brassy cough suggests tracheal compression
Postural cough with large sputum volumes → bronchiectasis
Cough with reflux symptoms or postnasal drip → the two great non-pulmonary causes of chronic cough
questions.red: New or changed cough >3 weeks in a smoker → exclude lung cancer.

followups.q: How long have you had it?
followups.probes: Under 3 weeks → usually infective · over 8 weeks → chronic cough, needs a systematic cause

followups.q: Do you cough anything up? How much a day — a teaspoon, an eggcup, a cupful? What colour?
followups.probes: Purulent with fever → infection · cupfuls, worse with position → bronchiectasis · mucoid most mornings in a smoker → chronic bronchitis

followups.q: Any blood in it, even streaks?
followups.probes: Any haemoptysis needs an explanation — cancer, TB and PE all sit here

followups.q: Is it worse at any particular time — at night, or first thing in the morning?
followups.probes: Night → asthma or reflux · early morning and productive → chronic bronchitis, bronchiectasis

followups.q: Any wheeze or tightness in the chest with it?
followups.probes: Points to obstruction — asthma or COPD

followups.q: Any fever, chills or night sweats? Have you become short of breath?
followups.probes: Fever → infective · new breathlessness → parenchymal disease, not just airway irritation

followups.q: Do you smoke or vape? Has a long-standing cough changed recently?
followups.probes: A new or changed cough in a smoker → exclude lung cancer

followups.q: Any new tablets, especially for blood pressure? Any heartburn, or a blocked, dripping nose?
followups.probes: ACE inhibitor, reflux and post-nasal drip — the three commonest causes of a chronic dry cough, all missed if you don't ask

questions.ask: Do you cough anything up? How much a day — a teaspoon, an eggcup? What colour?
questions.why: Volume and character localise the pathology. Patients rarely volunteer this — you must ask, and quantify in household measures.
points: Large volumes daily ("cupfuls"), especially postural → rules in bronchiectasis
Mucoid, chronic, worse in the mornings, in a smoker → chronic bronchitis
Foul-smelling, dark-coloured sputum → lung abscess with anaerobic organisms
Pink and frothy → pulmonary oedema — a cardiac answer hiding in a respiratory question
Rusty sputum → classic (if now uncommon) for pneumococcal pneumonia

followups.q: How much do you cough up in a day — a teaspoon, an eggcup, a cupful?
followups.probes: Quantify in household measures: cupfuls daily, especially worse with position, is the volume that rules in bronchiectasis

followups.q: What colour is it?
followups.probes: Yellow/green and purulent → infective · clear/white (mucoid) → chronic bronchitis or asthma · rusty → classic (if now rare) for pneumococcal pneumonia

followups.q: Does it smell foul?
followups.probes: Foul-smelling, dark-coloured sputum → lung abscess with anaerobic organisms

followups.q: Is there any blood in it?
followups.probes: Any streak of blood needs its own work-up — see the haemoptysis question

followups.q: Is it frothy and pink rather than a true sputum?
followups.probes: Pink frothy secretions are not sputum at all → pulmonary oedema, a cardiac answer hiding in a respiratory question

followups.q: Worse in the mornings, or worse lying on one side?
followups.probes: Morning-predominant in a smoker → chronic bronchitis · postural pooling → bronchiectasis

followups.q: Any fever with it?
followups.probes: Fever + purulent sputum → acute infective exacerbation or pneumonia

questions.ask: Do you ever hear a whistling sound when you breathe?
questions.why: Wheeze = airflow through narrowed lower airways, predominantly expiratory. It establishes obstructive physiology and, with pattern, splits asthma from COPD.
points: Episodic wheeze, diurnal variation (worse at night/early morning), triggers (exercise, cold, allergens, viral URTIs), atopy → rules in asthma
Fixed wheeze with chronic dyspnoea in a heavy smoker → COPD
Stridor — harsh, inspiratory, heard loudest over the trachea → upper airway obstruction (tumour, foreign body, anaphylaxis) — do not file this as wheeze; it's an emergency
New localised/monophonic wheeze in a smoker → single obstructed bronchus — think tumour or foreign body

followups.q: Does it come and go, or is it there all the time?
followups.probes: Episodic, variable → asthma · fixed and persistent → COPD

followups.q: What brings it on — exercise, cold air, allergens, colds?
followups.probes: Classic asthma triggers; also ask about hay fever and eczema (atopy)

followups.q: Is it worse at night or first thing in the morning?
followups.probes: Nocturnal or early-morning wheeze is a marker of poorly controlled asthma

followups.q: Is the noise loudest in your throat or neck, and is it worse breathing in or out?
followups.probes: Loudest over the trachea and worse on inspiration = stridor, not wheeze — upper airway obstruction, an emergency, not asthma/COPD

followups.q: Is it all over the chest, or in one spot, and is it a single note or many?
followups.probes: New, localised, single-pitch (monophonic) wheeze in a smoker → think an obstructing tumour or foreign body, not diffuse airway disease

questions.ask: Has your voice changed or become hoarse?
questions.why: A sneaky but crucial screen: the left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the aortic arch through the chest, so a left hilar/mediastinal lung cancer can present as a voice change (apical/Pancoast tumours instead cause Horner's syndrome and brachial-plexus signs). Persistent hoarseness >3 weeks needs laryngoscopy.
points: Hoarseness + smoking + cough/haemoptysis → rules in possible lung cancer or laryngeal cancer
Hoarseness after a URTI, resolving in days–weeks → laryngitis — benign
Hoarse voice in a heavy inhaled-corticosteroid user → local steroid effect/candida — check inhaler technique
questions.red: Persistent hoarseness >3 weeks needs laryngoscopy.

followups.q: How long has your voice been like this?
followups.probes: Days–weeks after a cold → laryngitis, benign · persistent beyond 3 weeks needs laryngoscopy

followups.q: Do you smoke? Any cough, or coughing up blood, with it?
followups.probes: Hoarseness + smoking + cough/haemoptysis → raises lung cancer (via recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement) or laryngeal cancer

followups.q: Do you use a steroid inhaler, and how do you use it?
followups.probes: Hoarse voice in a heavy inhaled-corticosteroid user → local steroid effect or oral candidiasis — check inhaler technique and spacer use

questions.ask: Do you get short of breath? How far on the flat? Compared with a year ago?
questions.why: The gas-exchange question. As with cardio, quantify exercise tolerance and establish trajectory. The tempo of onset is the key discriminator.
points: Minutes: pneumothorax, PE, foreign body, anaphylaxis, flash pulmonary oedema
Hours–days: pneumonia, asthma exacerbation, effusion accumulating
Months–years: COPD, pulmonary fibrosis (progressive, insidious), also anaemia and deconditioning
Episodic/variable with well periods between → asthma; fixed and progressive → COPD/fibrosis
Use the cardiac-vs-respiratory discriminator table in the cardio file — orthopnoea/PND/oedema pull cardiac; wheeze/sputum/smoking pull respiratory
Wakes at night breathless, or needs to sleep propped on pillows → orthopnoea/PND, pulling toward cardiac failure rather than primary lung disease
Sensation of not getting a satisfying breath in, with perioral/finger tingling → hyperventilation/anxiety, a diagnosis of exclusion
questions.red: Dyspnoea at rest, rapid progression, dyspnoea with stridor (upper airway obstruction — an emergency, not a wheeze).

followups.q: How long have you been short of breath — did it come on suddenly, over hours, or gradually over months?
followups.probes: Seconds–minutes → PE, pneumothorax, anaphylaxis, foreign body · hours–days → infection, asthma exacerbation, effusion · months–years → COPD, pulmonary fibrosis, anaemia, deconditioning

followups.q: How far can you walk on the flat, and how many stairs, before it stops you? How does that compare with a year ago?
followups.probes: Quantify in blocks/stairs and track the trajectory — more reliable than the patient's own grading of severity

followups.q: Do you ever wake at night breathless, or need to sleep propped up on pillows?
followups.probes: Orthopnoea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea point to left ventricular failure, not primary lung disease

followups.q: Any fever with it?
followups.probes: Fever → infective cause — pneumonia or an infective exacerbation

followups.q: Do you smoke?
followups.probes: Sets pre-test probability for COPD and lung cancer

followups.q: Any tightness in the chest when you're breathless?
followups.probes: Tightness → angina or asthma, depending on the rest of the story

followups.q: Any wheeze or cough with it?
followups.probes: Points to airways disease — asthma or COPD

followups.q: Does it feel like you can't get a satisfying breath in, with tingling round your lips or fingers?
followups.probes: Suggests hyperventilation/anxiety — a diagnosis of exclusion once organic causes are covered

questions.ask: Any sharp chest pain when you breathe in or cough?
questions.why: The lung itself is insensate — respiratory chest pain means pleural or chest wall involvement. Character separates it from cardiac pain.
points: Sharp, localised, worse on inspiration/coughing → pleuritic: PE, pneumonia reaching the pleura, pneumothorax, viral pleurisy
Sudden pleuritic pain + acute dyspnoea in a tall thin young smoker → spontaneous pneumothorax
Pleuritic pain + calf swelling/recent immobility → PE
Reproduced by palpation or twisting → chest wall/MSK (but exclude the above first)
Central, tight, exertional → back to the cardiac pathway

followups.q: Where exactly is the pain, and does it stay in one spot?
followups.probes: Localised, one-sided pain points to a pleural rather than a cardiac source

followups.q: Is it worse breathing in, or coughing?
followups.probes: Confirms a pleuritic pattern — pleura or chest wall, not the (insensate) lung itself

followups.q: Did it come on suddenly, and are you short of breath with it?
followups.probes: Sudden pleuritic pain + acute dyspnoea in a tall, thin, young smoker → spontaneous pneumothorax

followups.q: Any swelling or pain in a calf, recent surgery, a long flight or immobility?
followups.probes: Pleuritic pain + calf swelling/recent immobility → pulmonary embolism until excluded

followups.q: Does pressing on the area, or twisting your chest, reproduce it?
followups.probes: Reproducible on palpation points to a musculoskeletal cause — but only after PE, pneumothorax and pneumonia are excluded

questions.ask: Have you ever coughed up blood, even streaks?
questions.why: This is the highest-stakes question in the respiratory screen. Any haemoptysis needs an explanation; the differential includes three killers.
points: Haemoptysis + weight loss + smoking history → lung cancer until excluded
Haemoptysis + fever + night sweats ± TB contact/travel → tuberculosis
Sudden haemoptysis + pleuritic pain + dyspnoea ± recent surgery/immobility → pulmonary embolism
Blood-streaked purulent sputum during an infective exacerbation → usually infection/bronchiectasis — the common benign end of the spectrum
Confirm it's coughed, not vomited (haematemesis) or from the nose/gums — patients confuse these
Rapid, or over 250 mL in 24 hours → massive haemoptysis: a medical emergency needing immediate escalation, not just outpatient work-up
questions.red: The whole question is a red flag — never omit it, never ignore a positive.

followups.q: Are you sure it's coughed up, not vomited, or from your nose or gums?
followups.probes: Distinguishes true haemoptysis from haematemesis (follows nausea/retching, mixed with vomit) and nasopharyngeal bleeding (appears in the mouth, not mixed with sputum)

followups.q: How much — streaks, a teaspoon, or much more? How often?
followups.probes: Streaks/under 20 mL in 24h = mild · over 250 mL in 24h, or rapid, = massive haemoptysis, a medical emergency

followups.q: Do you smoke, and have you lost weight?
followups.probes: Haemoptysis + smoking + weight loss → lung cancer until excluded

followups.q: Any fever or drenching night sweats? Any TB contact or travel?
followups.probes: Fever, night sweats ± TB contact/travel → tuberculosis

followups.q: Did it come on suddenly, with breathlessness or sharp chest pain? Any recent surgery, long flight or immobility?
followups.probes: Sudden haemoptysis + pleuritic pain + dyspnoea ± immobility → pulmonary embolism

followups.q: Is it streaked through infected, purulent sputum?
followups.probes: Blood-streaked purulent sputum during an infective flare is usually the common, benign end of the spectrum — infection or bronchiectasis

followups.q: Any past TB, bronchiectasis or cystic fibrosis?
followups.probes: Known structural lung disease makes recurrent haemoptysis more likely from that same source — but still work it up fresh each time

questions.ask: Any fevers, shivers or drenching night sweats?
questions.why: Marks the process as infective or inflammatory, and drenching night sweats specifically flag the chronic granulomatous and malignant causes.
points: Acute fever + productive cough ± pleuritic pain → pneumonia
Drenching night sweats (change the sheets) + weight loss + chronic cough → TB or lymphoma — pair this with the travel/contact questions
Recurrent low-grade fevers with copious sputum → bronchiectasis exacerbations

followups.q: Is it a fever with shivers/rigors, or drenching sweats that soak the sheets at night?
followups.probes: Rigors point to bacteraemia/acute infection — drenching night sweats (changing the sheets) is the specific pattern that flags TB and lymphoma, not just feeling hot at night

followups.q: How long has this been going on?
followups.probes: Acute, short prodrome → bacterial pneumonia · longer prodrome over days → viral · weeks, with weight loss → TB, lymphoma

followups.q: Any cough, sputum or chest pain with it?
followups.probes: Fever + productive cough ± pleuritic pain → pneumonia

followups.q: Any weight loss, or contact with TB, or recent travel?
followups.probes: Adds to the TB/lymphoma picture — pursue with the weight-loss and exposure questions

followups.q: Do you have a chronic lung condition like bronchiectasis? Are these fevers low-grade and recurring?
followups.probes: Recurrent low-grade fevers with copious sputum in a known bronchiectatic → infective exacerbation

questions.ask: Have you lost weight without trying to? How much, and over how long?
questions.why: Unintentional weight loss reframes a respiratory symptom as systemic disease. Paired with cough, haemoptysis or night sweats, it moves malignancy and TB to the top of the differential.
points: Weight loss + haemoptysis + smoking history → lung cancer until excluded
Weight loss + drenching night sweats + chronic cough ± TB contact/travel → TB or lymphoma
Weight loss explained by reduced intake (anorexia, dysphagia, low mood) with no chest symptoms → look outside the respiratory system first
questions.red: Unintentional weight loss with any respiratory symptom is a red flag — quantify (kg and timeframe) and pursue to a cause.

followups.q: How much weight, and over how long?
followups.probes: Quantify in kg and timeframe — unintentional loss of >5% body weight over 6–12 months is what makes this significant

followups.q: Is it definitely unintentional — appetite, diet and activity unchanged?
followups.probes: Confirms it's not simply reduced intake or increased exercise before chasing an organic cause

followups.q: Any cough, haemoptysis or smoking history?
followups.probes: Weight loss + haemoptysis + smoking → lung cancer until excluded

followups.q: Any night sweats, or TB contact/travel?
followups.probes: Weight loss + drenching night sweats + chronic cough ± TB contact/travel → TB or lymphoma

followups.q: Any reason you might be eating less — appetite, swallowing, mood?
followups.probes: Weight loss explained by reduced intake with no chest symptoms points outside the respiratory system entirely

questions.ask: Do you smoke, or ever? What work have you done over your life? Pets, birds, recent travel, TB contact?
questions.why: The lung is the organ most exposed to the environment — a respiratory history without an exposure history is half a history. This sets pre-test probability just as the risk-factor screen does in cardio.
points: Smoking: quantify in pack-years (packs/day × years); never smoked / ex (when quit) / current

Occupation — lifetime, not just current (asbestos disease often appears decades later, commonly 20–40+ years): mining/quarrying and engineered/artificial-stone benchtop work (silicosis — the current high-yield Australian exposure; the product was banned in Australia in 2024), construction/shipyards/insulation (asbestos → mesothelioma), farming (hypersensitivity pneumonitis), baking/spray-painting (occupational asthma — ask if symptoms improve on holidays)
Travel/TB contact: TB, but also endemic mycoses depending on geography
Medications: amiodarone, methotrexate, nitrofurantoin (pulmonary fibrosis); ACE inhibitor (cough); beta-blockers (bronchospasm)

followups.q: How many cigarettes or packs a day, and for how many years — or when did you quit?
followups.probes: Quantify in pack-years (packs/day × years) — the single most useful number for COPD and lung cancer risk

followups.q: What jobs have you done across your whole working life, not just now?
followups.probes: Ask lifetime exposure — asbestos disease and silicosis can surface 20–40 years after exposure ended

followups.q: Any work with stone benchtops, mining, quarrying, construction, shipyards or insulation?
followups.probes: Engineered/artificial stone cutting → silicosis (Australia's current high-yield exposure, product banned 2024) · asbestos trades → asbestosis/mesothelioma, latency up to 30 years

followups.q: Any pets or birds at home, or work with animals?
followups.probes: Bird fancier's lung, psittacosis, Q fever

followups.q: Any recent travel, or contact with someone with TB?
followups.probes: Sets pre-test probability for TB and endemic mycoses by geography

followups.q: Do your symptoms get better on holidays or over the weekend, away from work?
followups.probes: Improvement away from work is the classic clue to occupational asthma — commonly from spray paints, flour dust or soldering fumes

followups.q: Any medications — amiodarone, methotrexate, nitrofurantoin, ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers?
followups.probes: Amiodarone/methotrexate/nitrofurantoin → pulmonary fibrosis · ACE inhibitor → cough · beta-blocker → bronchospasm

questions.ask: Do you snore heavily? Has anyone seen you stop breathing in your sleep? Do you fall asleep by day — even driving?
questions.why: Obstructive sleep apnoea is common, underdiagnosed, and dangerous (motor vehicle accidents, resistant hypertension, AF). The best historian is the bed partner.
points: Loud snoring + witnessed apnoeas + unrefreshing sleep + daytime somnolence (especially while driving) → rules in OSA — refer for a sleep study
Distinguish from PND (wakes gasping but from pulmonary oedema, with other failure symptoms) and simple poor sleep hygiene

followups.q: Has anyone seen you stop breathing, choke or gasp in your sleep?
followups.probes: Witnessed apnoea/choking is a more reliable sign of OSA than snoring alone — snoring is common without OSA

followups.q: Do you wake unrefreshed, or fall asleep during the day — reading, watching TV, or driving?
followups.probes: Daytime somnolence, especially at the wheel, is what makes this dangerous (motor vehicle accidents) and worth a sleep study

followups.q: Are you waking breathless and needing to sit up, or is it more that you're gasping/snoring through the night?
followups.probes: Distinguishes OSA from paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea (cardiac failure) — PND wakes the patient gasping with other symptoms of failure, not snoring

followups.q: Any high blood pressure that's hard to control, or an irregular heartbeat?
followups.probes: OSA is linked to resistant hypertension and atrial fibrillation — worth flagging even if sleep itself isn't the presenting complaint

systems.drill: AIRWAY: cough, sputum (volume + colour), wheeze, hoarseness · AIR SACS: dyspnoea + exercise tolerance · LINING: pleuritic chest pain · SINISTER: haemoptysis, fever/night sweats, weight loss · CONTEXT: smoking (pack-years), occupation, pets/travel/TB contact, snoring/daytime sleepiness
systems.clnote: See also ENT — epistaxis, hoarseness, URTI symptoms (sore throat, runny nose, painful ears).

systems.name: Gastrointestinal
systems.scaffoldIntro: Follow the food from mouth to anus — the GI screen is literally a journey down the tube:
systems.scaffoldOutro: Move top-to-bottom and you cannot forget a segment. Two red-flag threads run the whole length: **bleeding** (haematemesis at the top → melaena → fresh PR blood at the bottom) and **obstruction/malignancy** (dysphagia at the top → change in bowel habit at the bottom).

questions.ask: Any difficulty swallowing? Does food or drink stick — solids, liquids, or both?
questions.why: Dysphagia is always significant and the solid-vs-liquid pattern localises the lesion.
points: Solids first, progressing to liquids → mechanical obstruction: oesophageal cancer (esp. with weight loss, older, smoker/drinker) or benign stricture
Solids and liquids from the start → motility disorder (achalasia, neuromuscular)
Difficulty initiating the swallow with coughing/nasal regurgitation → oropharyngeal/neurological (stroke, bulbar)
questions.red: Progressive dysphagia + weight loss → oesophageal cancer until excluded.

followups.q: Do you have trouble with solids, liquids, or both?
followups.probes: Solids only → mechanical (cancer, stricture) · solids and liquids together → a motor problem (achalasia, spasm)

followups.q: Where does it feel like it's sticking — can you point?
followups.probes: Pointing to the lower oesophagus supports a mechanical obstruction there — but referred sensation is unreliable for lesions higher up

followups.q: Is it constant, or does it come and go — worse with the first few mouthfuls?
followups.probes: Intermittent, or worse on first swallows, → eosinophilic oesophagitis, a lower oesophageal ring, or (rarely) diffuse oesophageal spasm

followups.q: Has it been getting steadily worse?
followups.probes: Progressive difficulty → stricture, carcinoma, or achalasia

followups.q: Do you cough or choke as you start to swallow, or does fluid come back up your nose?
followups.probes: Suggests oropharyngeal dysphagia — a pharyngeal or neurological (bulbar) cause, not an oesophageal one

followups.q: Is it painful to swallow?
followups.probes: Odynophagia suggests acute inflammation — infective oesophagitis (Candida, herpes), a lodged pill, or caustic injury

followups.q: Any heartburn or acid regurgitation with it?
followups.probes: Supports GORD, with or without a peptic stricture, as the cause

followups.q: Have you lost weight? Do you have asthma or hay fever?
followups.probes: Weight loss raises concern for cancer; atopy supports eosinophilic oesophagitis

questions.ask: Any heartburn, acid reflux, or burning discomfort in the upper abdomen?
questions.why: Very common; the job is to separate benign reflux from the ulcers and the cancers.
points: Retrosternal burning, worse lying flat/after meals, relieved by antacids → GORD

Epigastric pain related to meals → peptic ulcer (the classic "duodenal relieved by food, gastric worsened by it" pattern is unreliable — Talley: duodenal and gastric ulcers can't be distinguished clinically, and pain isn't always meal-related)

Dyspepsia + ALARM features (Anaemia, Loss of weight, Anorexia, Recent onset/progressive, Melaena/haematemesis, Swallowing difficulty) → urgent endoscopy for gastric cancer (Talley's core alarm set is the four: dysphagia, weight loss, melaena, haematemesis)
Radiates across the chest, down the arm, or into the jaw → raises myocardial ischaemia instead of reflux
questions.red: ALARM: Anaemia, Loss of weight, Anorexia, Recent/progressive onset, Melaena/haematemesis, Swallowing difficulty.

followups.q: How often does this happen — more than once a week?
followups.probes: More than weekly supports a diagnosis of GORD rather than occasional reflux

followups.q: Does it come on after meals, or when you bend forward or lie flat?
followups.probes: Typical triggers for acid reflux

followups.q: Does it radiate across your chest, down your arm, or into your jaw?
followups.probes: Raises concern for myocardial ischaemia rather than reflux — don't anchor on GORD until this is excluded

followups.q: Is it relieved by antacids, or does it come with a sudden rush of bitter fluid into your mouth?
followups.probes: Relief with antacids and true acid regurgitation both support reflux; a salty or tasteless fluid instead is waterbrash, not GORD

followups.q: Any trouble swallowing, weight loss, or black stools/vomited blood with it?
followups.probes: The ALARM features that mean this isn't straightforward reflux and needs endoscopy

questions.ask: Any nausea or vomiting? How often, and what seems to trigger it?
questions.why: Timing and content localise the cause — early-morning vomiting points away from the gut itself.
points: Vomiting + colicky pain + distension + absolute constipation → bowel obstruction
Faeculent vomiting → distal/large bowel obstruction or fistula
Early morning vomiting → raised ICP, pregnancy, alcohol

followups.q: Does it happen right after eating, or hours later?
followups.probes: Delayed more than an hour after meals → gastric outlet obstruction or gastroparesis · early morning, before eating, → pregnancy, alcohol, or raised intracranial pressure

followups.q: What does the vomit look like — bile-stained, old food, or blood?
followups.probes: Bile → an open duodenal–gastric connection · old food → outlet obstruction · blood → ulceration, needing its own work-up

followups.q: Any abdominal pain, colicky pain with distension, or absence of flatus?
followups.probes: Points towards bowel obstruction rather than a primary vomiting disorder

followups.q: Is it actually vomiting, or does food come back up effortlessly and get re-swallowed or spat out?
followups.probes: Effortless regurgitation of recently eaten food is rumination, not true vomiting — a different diagnosis entirely

followups.q: Any headaches, or is this a recurring pattern with well periods in between?
followups.probes: Worsening headaches raise raised intracranial pressure; distinct well-then-vomiting cycles suggest cyclical vomiting syndrome

questions.ask: What does the vomit look like — any blood or coffee-grounds?
questions.why: Haematemesis is a red flag on its own — it always needs an upper GI source excluded, and the character (fresh blood vs coffee-grounds) hints at the rate of bleeding.
points: Haematemesis / coffee-ground vomit → upper GI bleed (ulcer, varices, Mallory–Weiss); ask about NSAIDs, alcohol, known liver disease
questions.red: Haematemesis — ask about NSAIDs, alcohol, known liver disease.

followups.q: Was it fresh red blood, or did it look like coffee grounds?
followups.probes: Fresh blood suggests a brisk, ongoing bleed; coffee-grounds suggests blood altered by acid — a slower or older bleed

followups.q: Did the blood come with the first vomit, or only after repeated retching?
followups.probes: Blood appearing only after several episodes of clear vomiting suggests a Mallory–Weiss tear rather than a primary ulcer bleed

followups.q: Are you on aspirin, NSAIDs, or steroids, and do you drink alcohol or have known liver disease?
followups.probes: The core risk factors for peptic ulcer bleeding and for varices

questions.ask: Any tummy pain? Where exactly? Any bloating or fullness after meals?
questions.why: Site and character map onto the organ and process — characterise fully with SOCRATES. Bloating/postprandial fullness point to functional or gastric causes.
points: RUQ/epigastric, typically constant and severe for hours (Talley: biliary pain is "rarely colicky"; the fatty-food trigger is unpredictable) → biliary pain/cholecystitis; constant + fever + jaundice → cholangitis
Epigastric boring to the back, relieved leaning forward → pancreatitis; also peptic ulcer, AAA
Loin to groin, colicky, can't stay still → renal colic
Central, poorly localised, then localising → the visceral-to-parietal progression of many surgical abdomens
questions.red: Sudden "worst ever" + shock → perforation, ruptured AAA, mesenteric ischaemia, ruptured ectopic.

followups.q: Can you point to exactly where it is, and does it move anywhere else?
followups.probes: Site follows embryological origin — epigastric (foregut), periumbilical (midgut), suprapubic (hindgut); radiation to the back suggests pancreas, to the scapula suggests gallbladder/diaphragm

followups.q: Does it come in waves, or is it constant?
followups.probes: Colicky (waves) → obstruction (bowel, ureter) · steady/constant → inflammation or ischaemia

followups.q: Is it related to eating — worse after meals, or when fasting?
followups.probes: Meal-related epigastric pain suggests peptic disease, though the link isn't reliable; pain specifically provoked by eating can also be intestinal ischaemia

followups.q: Do you feel better moving around, or do you want to lie perfectly still?
followups.probes: Restlessness/rolling around → colicky pain (obstruction); lying still, reluctant to move → peritonitis

followups.q: Does passing wind or a bowel motion ease it?
followups.probes: Temporary relief with defecation/flatus points to colonic disease

followups.q: Any fever, jaundice, or vomiting with it?
followups.probes: Fever + jaundice + RUQ pain → cholangitis; vomiting is common with biliary and pancreatic pain

followups.q: Did it come on suddenly and severely — the worst pain you've ever had?
followups.probes: Sudden, maximal-at-onset, severe pain with shock → perforation, ruptured AAA, mesenteric ischaemia, ruptured ectopic

followups.q: Any change in bowel habit, blood in the stool, or weight loss alongside it?
followups.probes: Reframes chronic abdominal pain as a possible malignancy work-up rather than a functional one

questions.ask: How is your appetite? Any weight loss?
questions.why: Ties GI complaints to the constitutional malignancy screen; weight loss escalates the urgency of every symptom above.
points: Anorexia + weight loss together → raises suspicion of underlying malignancy (but also occurs in depression and other disease)
Weight loss with an increased appetite → malabsorption or a hypermetabolic state, e.g. thyrotoxicosis
Early satiety/postprandial fullness without weight loss → functional dyspepsia

followups.q: Has your appetite changed — more, less, or the same?
followups.probes: Loss of appetite + weight loss raises concern for malignancy; weight loss with an increased appetite suggests malabsorption or a hypermetabolic state (e.g. thyrotoxicosis)

followups.q: How much weight, and over what period?
followups.probes: Quantify — document onset and rate; rapid, unintentional loss is what escalates urgency

followups.q: Do you fill up quickly, or feel uncomfortably full after normal-sized meals?
followups.probes: Early satiety/postprandial fullness can be gastric cancer, peptic ulcer, or functional dyspepsia

followups.q: Any change in how food tastes, or reason you might be eating less — low mood, dentition, swallowing?
followups.probes: Taste disturbance can occur with liver disease; screens for non-GI explanations before assuming malignancy

questions.ask: Have your bowels changed — more or less often, looser or harder than normal for you?
questions.why: "Normal" is individual, so anchor to the patient's baseline. A persistent change is a cancer screen.
