points: Persistent change (esp. looser/more frequent) + weight loss + PR bleeding, especially in an older adult → colorectal cancer until excluded (symptomatic suspicion is age-independent; note Australia's bowel-screening age is now 45)
Diarrhoea + blood + mucus + urgency + systemic upset in a young patient → IBD

Alternating constipation/diarrhoea with pain relieved by defecation, no red flags → IBS — a positive diagnosis on the Rome criteria (recurrent abdominal pain ≥1 day/week for 3 months + ≥2 of: related to defecation, change in stool frequency, change in stool form), no longer a diagnosis of exclusion

followups.q: What's changed, exactly — more or less often, looser or harder, compared to your normal?
followups.probes: Anchor to the patient's own baseline — "normal" is individual

followups.q: How long has this been going on, and did it come on suddenly or gradually?
followups.probes: Acute → more likely infective; chronic/persistent needs a systematic work-up

followups.q: Any blood, mucus, or pus in the stool? Do you have to rush to the toilet?
followups.probes: Blood/mucus/pus and urgency point to colonic inflammation — IBD or infective colitis

followups.q: Any weight loss, or waking at night specifically because of your bowels?
followups.probes: Weight loss or nocturnal symptoms are organic red flags — they don't fit a purely functional diagnosis

followups.q: Any recent antibiotics, or travel?
followups.probes: Antibiotics → consider C. difficile; travel → consider Giardia and other infective causes

followups.q: Is any pain relieved by opening your bowels, and does it come with bloating or a feeling of incomplete emptying?
followups.probes: Supports IBS by the Rome criteria — a positive diagnosis, not one of exclusion, once red flags are absent

followups.q: Any family history of bowel cancer, coeliac disease, or inflammatory bowel disease?
followups.probes: Shifts pre-test probability and may prompt earlier investigation

followups.q: Any joint pains, mouth ulcers, or eye redness alongside the bowel symptoms?
followups.probes: Extra-intestinal features support inflammatory bowel disease

questions.ask: Any blood when you go to the toilet — bright red, or black and tarry?
questions.why: Colour tells you the level of the bleed.
points: Melaena (black, tarry, offensive) → upper GI bleed — pair with the haematemesis question
Bright red coating the stool / on the paper → anorectal (haemorrhoids, fissure)
Blood mixed through the stool + change in habit + weight loss → colorectal cancer

followups.q: Is the blood bright red or black and tarry?
followups.probes: Bright red → usually a lower source · black, tarry, offensive (melaena) → usually an upper GI bleed

followups.q: Is it on the paper/coating the stool, or mixed all through it?
followups.probes: On the surface/paper → anorectal (haemorrhoids, fissure) · mixed through the stool → a more proximal colonic source, including cancer

followups.q: Any change in bowel habit or weight loss alongside it?
followups.probes: Blood + altered habit + weight loss → colorectal cancer until excluded

followups.q: Have you vomited any blood or coffee-ground material?
followups.probes: Pairs melaena with the haematemesis question — confirms an upper GI source

followups.q: Any abdominal pain with it?
followups.probes: Painless vs pain-associated bleeding narrows the differential (e.g. painless diverticular bleed vs painful colitis)

followups.q: Any family or personal history of polyps, bowel cancer, or inflammatory bowel disease?
followups.probes: Raises pre-test probability and may change the urgency of investigation

followups.q: Are you on aspirin, other blood thinners, or NSAIDs?
followups.probes: These provoke and worsen GI bleeding from any source and change the immediate risk

questions.ask: Any mucus or slime with your stool?
questions.why: Mucus with blood and diarrhoea points to mucosal inflammation rather than a purely mechanical or bleeding cause.
points: Bloody diarrhoea with mucus → colitis (IBD or infective)

questions.ask: Is the stool pale, greasy, or hard to flush?
questions.why: Pale, greasy, floating stool means fat isn't being absorbed — the fat itself is passing through undigested.
points: Pale, greasy, floating, hard-to-flush stool → fat malabsorption (pancreatic insufficiency, biliary obstruction, coeliac disease)

followups.q: Do you see oil droplets in the toilet, or does the stool float and stick to the bowl?
followups.probes: Oil droplets suggest chronic pancreatitis specifically; floating and hard-to-flush is the general fat-malabsorption pattern

followups.q: Any weight loss, or a personal/family history of coeliac disease?
followups.probes: Helps distinguish pancreatic insufficiency, biliary obstruction, and coeliac disease as the three big causes

questions.ask: Any yellowing of your eyes or skin?
questions.why: Jaundice is the headline sign of hepatobiliary disease — the accompanying urine/stool/itch pattern (asked next) tells you which type before any blood test.
points: Jaundice + risk factors (alcohol, viral hepatitis, paracetamol, travel) + systemic upset → hepatic
Fever + abdominal pain + jaundice → cholangitis, needs urgent treatment
Painless jaundice + weight loss → think pancreatic head cancer (Courvoisier) until excluded

followups.q: Is your urine darker than usual, and are your stools pale?
followups.probes: Dark urine + pale stools → an obstructive (post-hepatic) picture

followups.q: Any itching?
followups.probes: Itch tracks with the same cholestatic/obstructive picture

followups.q: Any fever, or abdominal pain?
followups.probes: Fever + RUQ pain + jaundice → cholangitis, needs urgent treatment

followups.q: Any change in appetite or weight loss?
followups.probes: Painless jaundice with weight loss raises pancreatic head cancer (Courvoisier)

followups.q: Any vomiting blood, or black stools?
followups.probes: Suggests coagulopathy from liver disease, or a separate GI bleed — needs its own work-up

followups.q: How much alcohol do you drink, and for how long? Any past hepatitis, or new medications?
followups.probes: The core drug/alcohol/viral triad for a hepatic cause

followups.q: Any tattoos, IV drug use, blood transfusions, or high-risk sexual contact?
followups.probes: Risk factors for viral hepatitis B/C

followups.q: Any recent travel to areas where hepatitis is common?
followups.probes: Hepatitis A exposure risk

questions.ask: Any change in the colour of your urine or stool — dark urine, pale or clay-coloured stool?
questions.why: Conjugated bilirubin being shunted into the urine instead of the gut is the signature of obstructive (post-hepatic) jaundice.
points: Dark urine + pale stools → obstructive (post-hepatic) jaundice: gallstones, or if painless with weight loss, pancreatic head cancer (Courvoisier)

followups.q: Any yellowing of your eyes or skin, or itching?
followups.probes: Confirms this sits within the same obstructive/cholestatic picture as jaundice, rather than an isolated urine colour change

followups.q: Any abdominal pain, or unexplained weight loss?
followups.probes: Painful → gallstones; painless with weight loss → think pancreatic head cancer (Courvoisier)

questions.ask: Any itching, especially generalised?
questions.why: Retained bile salts under the skin cause the itch of cholestasis — it tracks with the same obstructive picture as dark urine and pale stool.
points: Generalised itch with jaundice → cholestasis (obstructive or hepatic)

followups.q: Is it generalised, or worse in particular areas — like your hands and feet?
followups.probes: Generalised itch, worse over the extremities, is typical of cholestatic liver disease

followups.q: Any yellowing of the eyes/skin, dark urine, or pale stools with it?
followups.probes: Confirms the cholestatic picture rather than a primary skin cause (eczema, scabies, dry skin)

systems.drill: **TOP:** dysphagia (solids→liquids?), heartburn/dyspepsia (ALARM?), nausea/vomiting (blood?), haematemesis · **MIDDLE:** abdominal pain (SOCRATES + site), appetite/weight · **BOTTOM:** change in bowel habit, PR bleeding/melaena, mucus · **OUTSIDE:** jaundice + dark urine/pale stool/itch

discriminator.title: upper vs lower GI bleed
rows: Fresh or dark red PR blood
Change in bowel habit, weight loss
A brisk upper GI bleed can present as fresh PR blood + shock

systems.seeAlso: Haematological — GI blood loss is the commonest cause of iron-deficiency anaemia

systems.name: Genitourinary / Renal
systems.scaffoldIntro: Follow the urine from kidney to outside, splitting the lower-tract symptoms into the two classic groups, then finish on renal failure:

chunks.gen: Hesitancy, poor stream, dribbling, pis-en-deux, retention

systems.scaffoldOutro: The **storage (irritative) vs voiding (obstructive)** split is the key LUTS framework: storage symptoms point to the bladder itself (infection, overactivity), voiding symptoms point to outflow obstruction (prostate). Haematuria is the red-flag thread throughout.
systems.seeAlso: Reproductive & Sexual History — menstrual, pelvic, testicular, STI questions (the two overlap at dysuria and discharge)

questions.ask: How often do you pass urine? Do you have to rush? Up at night — how many times?
questions.why: Frequency, urgency and nocturia together define an irritable/overactive bladder or infection.
points: + polyuria + polydipsia + weight loss → screen for diabetes
Nocturia alone → also cardiac failure (nocturnal fluid redistribution) and, in older men, prostatic disease
Fever + loin pain alongside storage symptoms → upper tract involvement (pyelonephritis), not simple cystitis

followups.q: How many times a day, and how many times overnight?
followups.probes: Quantify frequency and nocturia — the baseline to track change and severity

followups.q: Do you get a sudden strong urge that's hard to hold on, or is it more just going often?
followups.probes: Urgency implies detrusor overactivity/overactive bladder rather than simple frequency

followups.q: Any burning or stinging when you go, or cloudy/smelly urine?
followups.probes: Dysuria + cloudy urine → UTI

followups.q: Are you drinking more, or losing weight without trying?
followups.probes: Polyuria + polydipsia + weight loss → screen for diabetes

followups.q: Any breathlessness, ankle swelling, or known heart failure?
followups.probes: Nocturia alone can be nocturnal fluid redistribution from cardiac failure, not a bladder problem

followups.q: In men — any trouble starting, weak stream, or a feeling of not emptying alongside this?
followups.probes: Combined storage + voiding symptoms in an older man points to prostatic outflow obstruction

followups.q: Any fever, loin pain, or feeling generally unwell?
followups.probes: Suggests upper tract involvement (pyelonephritis) rather than simple cystitis

questions.ask: Do you ever leak urine? With coughing/laughing, or with a sudden urge you can’t defer?
questions.why: The trigger separates two mechanisms with opposite treatments.
points: Leak on coughing/laughing/lifting → stress incontinence (pelvic floor)
Leak preceded by a sudden unstoppable urge → urge incontinence (overactive bladder)
Continuous dribble → overflow (chronic retention) or fistula
questions.red: New incontinence + back pain + saddle anaesthesia + bilateral leg symptoms → cauda equina.

followups.q: Does it leak with coughing, laughing, sneezing or lifting, or with a sudden urge you can't defer?
followups.probes: Leak with raised intra-abdominal pressure → stress incontinence; leak preceded by urge → urge incontinence (overactive bladder) — opposite mechanisms, opposite treatments

followups.q: Is it a small squirt, or does it empty the whole bladder?
followups.probes: Small squirts → stress · larger volume, may empty the bladder → urge

followups.q: Is it more a continuous dribble, especially after you think you've finished?
followups.probes: Continuous dribble suggests overflow (chronic retention) or, rarely, a fistula — a different mechanism again

followups.q: Any back pain, numbness around the saddle area, or weakness/numbness in the legs with it?
followups.probes: New incontinence + back pain + saddle anaesthesia + bilateral leg symptoms → cauda equina, a surgical emergency

followups.q: Did this start after a delivery, around menopause, or with a new medical problem or medication?
followups.probes: Pelvic floor trauma and oestrogen withdrawal point to stress incontinence; a new neurological trigger or medication points elsewhere

questions.ask: Trouble starting? Weak stream? Dribble at the end, feel you haven’t emptied, or need to go again straight away?
questions.why: Hesitancy, poor stream, terminal dribbling, pis-en-deux (double voiding — passing urine, then needing to go again minutes later) and incomplete emptying are the classic outflow obstruction cluster — in older men that means the prostate.
points: Voiding LUTS in an older man → BPH; with weight loss/bone pain/haematuria → exclude prostate cancer
Complete inability to pass urine + painful distended bladder → acute urinary retention (emergency)
Painless retention with overflow incontinence → chronic retention/neurogenic bladder
questions.red: Acute urinary retention is an emergency.

followups.q: Is it hard to start, and does the stream come out weak or interrupted?
followups.probes: Hesitancy + poor/intermittent stream are the earliest outflow-obstruction symptoms

followups.q: Does it dribble at the end, and do you feel you've fully emptied?
followups.probes: Terminal dribbling and a sense of incomplete emptying complete the classic BPH picture

followups.q: Do you need to go again just minutes after you've just been?
followups.probes: Pis-en-deux (double voiding) is a specific marker of incomplete emptying from outflow obstruction

followups.q: Are you completely unable to pass urine, with a painful, swollen lower tummy?
followups.probes: Complete retention with a painful distended bladder is acute urinary retention — an emergency

followups.q: Any blood in the urine, bone pain, or weight loss alongside this?
followups.probes: In an older man these symptoms should prompt excluding prostate cancer, not just assuming benign hypertrophy

followups.q: Is the dribbling painless and continuous, without you noticing the urge?
followups.probes: Painless overflow incontinence without sensation suggests chronic retention or a neurogenic bladder rather than simple BPH

followups.q: Any fevers or recurrent infections alongside these symptoms?
followups.probes: Obstruction predisposes to urinary infection — treat the obstruction, not just the infection, or it will recur

questions.ask: Any pain or burning when you pass urine?
questions.why: The cardinal symptom of lower urinary tract infection/inflammation.
points: + fever + loin pain + rigors → pyelonephritis (upper tract — more serious)
+ urethral/vaginal discharge + sexual history → STI (cross-reference the reproductive history)

followups.q: Any need to go more often, or urgently, with it?
followups.probes: Dysuria + frequency + urgency + suprapubic pain → cystitis/UTI

followups.q: Any fever, chills/rigors, or pain in your back or side?
followups.probes: Fever + loin pain + rigors → pyelonephritis, the more serious upper-tract infection

followups.q: Any discharge from the urethra or vagina, and are you sexually active?
followups.probes: Discharge + a relevant sexual history → consider an STI rather than a straightforward UTI

followups.q: Is the burning at the start of your stream, or throughout/at the end?
followups.probes: Burning right at the start, clearing after, points more to a urethral cause; burning throughout suggests cystitis

questions.ask: Have you ever seen blood in your urine?
questions.why: The GU red flag. Any visible haematuria needs an explanation — the differential includes urological cancers.
points: Painless visible haematuria → bladder/renal cancer until excluded (esp. older, smoker)
Within a few days of a sore throat (synpharyngitic) → IgA nephropathy; ~1–2 weeks after a throat/skin infection, with hypertension/oedema → post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis
Confirm it isn't menstrual, dietary (beetroot), or drug-related (rifampicin) discolouration
questions.red: Painless visible haematuria is cancer until excluded.

followups.q: Was the blood visible to you, or was this picked up on a test?
followups.probes: Visible (macroscopic) haematuria carries a much higher cancer risk than an incidental finding of microscopic blood — investigate both, but with different urgency

followups.q: Is it painful, or completely painless?
followups.probes: Painless visible haematuria → bladder/renal cancer until excluded, especially in an older smoker

followups.q: Any colicky loin-to-groin pain with it?
followups.probes: Colicky pain alongside blood points to a ureteric stone rather than malignancy

followups.q: Any burning, frequency, or fever with it?
followups.probes: Suggests a UTI as the source rather than a structural or malignant cause

followups.q: Did this start within a few days of a sore throat, or 1–2 weeks after a throat or skin infection?
followups.probes: Days after a sore throat (synpharyngitic) → IgA nephropathy · 1–2 weeks after, with hypertension/oedema, → post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis

followups.q: Could this be your period, something you've eaten like beetroot, or a new medication like rifampicin?
followups.probes: Rules out the mimics before committing to a true haematuria work-up

followups.q: Do you smoke, and have you lost weight?
followups.probes: The classic risk profile for urothelial and renal malignancy

followups.q: Are you on blood thinners, or have you had a recent catheter, procedure, or injury?
followups.probes: Anticoagulation and instrumentation are common, less sinister explanations — but painless haematuria should still be investigated even on anticoagulants

questions.ask: Any change in the colour, smell, or how frothy your urine is? How much are you passing?
questions.why: Frothiness and smell add renal clues beyond blood alone.
points: Frothy urine → significant proteinuria (nephrotic range); offensive smell → infection

followups.q: Is it frothy, tea-coloured, or does it have an unusual smell?
followups.probes: Persistent froth → significant proteinuria (nephrotic range); offensive smell → infection

followups.q: How much are you passing overall — more than usual, or noticeably less?
followups.probes: Very little (oliguria/anuria) raises acute kidney injury; unusually large volumes raise diabetes or a concentrating defect

questions.ask: Any pain in your back or side, below the ribs?
questions.why: Localises disease to the kidney/ureter.
points: Severe colicky loin-to-groin, patient writhing → ureteric stone
Constant loin pain + fever + rigors → pyelonephritis
Dull bilateral loin ache → obstruction, polycystic kidneys

followups.q: Is it colicky — coming in waves — or a constant ache?
followups.probes: Colicky, severe, patient writhing → ureteric stone; constant → infection or obstruction

followups.q: Does it radiate anywhere — down towards the groin or testis?
followups.probes: Loin-to-groin radiation is classic for a ureteric stone tracking down the ureter

followups.q: Any fever, rigors, or feeling generally unwell with it?
followups.probes: Constant loin pain + fever + rigors → pyelonephritis

followups.q: Is it on one side, or a dull ache on both sides?
followups.probes: Dull bilateral loin ache raises obstruction or polycystic kidneys rather than a single stone

followups.q: Any family history of kidney problems, or high blood pressure?
followups.probes: Family history of enlarged kidneys and hypertension → polycystic kidney disease

questions.ask: Any swelling, especially around the eyes or ankles?
questions.why: Fluid retention from a failing kidney has a nephrotic (heavy proteinuria, periorbital) or nephritic (salt/water retention) pattern.

followups.q: Is it around your eyes in the morning, or more in your ankles by evening?
followups.probes: Periorbital swelling suggests a nephrotic (heavy proteinuria) pattern; ankle swelling worse by evening is a more generalised fluid-retention pattern

followups.q: Is your urine frothy, and have you noticed weight gain?
followups.probes: Oedema + frothy urine → a nephrotic/nephritic picture rather than a cardiac or hepatic cause

questions.ask: Any generalised itching, easy bruising, or persistent hiccups?
questions.why: As the kidneys fail, retained toxins produce a quiet cluster that's easy to miss unless you ask for it specifically.
points: Generalised itch (pruritus) + easy bruising + hiccups + nausea + fatigue → uraemia (advanced renal failure)
Reduced urine output (oliguria/anuria) → acute kidney injury — look for the cause (pre-renal, renal, post-renal)

followups.q: Any nausea, poor appetite, or unusual tiredness alongside this?
followups.probes: Completes the uraemic cluster — itch, bruising, hiccups, nausea and fatigue together suggest advanced renal failure

followups.q: How much urine are you passing overall?
followups.probes: A marked reduction (oliguria/anuria) points to acute kidney injury — look for a pre-renal, renal, or post-renal cause

followups.q: Do you know your kidney function results — creatinine or eGFR?
followups.probes: Many patients already know this number and it tells you how advanced the picture is before you order anything

systems.drill: **STORAGE:** frequency, urgency, nocturia, incontinence (stress vs urge) · **VOIDING:** hesitancy, poor stream, dribbling, pis-en-deux, retention · **CONTENT:** dysuria, haematuria (painless = red flag), appearance (frothy/offensive), volume, loin pain · **RENAL FAILURE:** oedema, itch, bruising, hiccups · **plus** the Reproductive & Sexual History screen alongside
systems.clnote: Ask the Reproductive & Sexual History screen alongside this one.

discriminator.title: stress vs urge incontinence
rows: Cough, laugh, sneeze, lift (raised intra-abdominal pressure)

systems.name: Neurological
systems.scaffoldIntro: Work from the top of the neuraxis down, then out to the special senses:

chunks.gen: Vision, hearing, swallowing, facial weakness, smell

systems.scaffoldOutro: The single most useful discriminator running through the whole system is the tempo of onset: sudden (seconds–minutes) → vascular (stroke, haemorrhage, SAH); subacute (days–weeks) → inflammatory/infective/compressive; chronic (months–years) → degenerative/neoplastic.

questions.ask: Has anyone noticed you seem more confused than usual — coming and going, or constant?
questions.why: Fluctuating confusion over hours–days is delirium until an underlying systemic cause is found; a gradual, non-fluctuating decline points instead to dementia.
points: Acute confusion over hours–days, fluctuating, ± reversed sleep–wake → delirium — look for the systemic cause (infection, drugs, metabolic)

followups.q: Did this come on suddenly, over hours to days, and does it come and go through the day?
followups.probes: Acute, fluctuating, often worse at night → delirium; gradual and steady over months → dementia instead

followups.q: Any fever, new medications, or recent illness?
followups.probes: Delirium always has an underlying trigger — infection, drugs, or a metabolic disturbance — go looking for it rather than treating confusion as the diagnosis

followups.q: Has anyone else noticed this — family, carers?
followups.probes: A collateral history is often more reliable than the patient's own account, especially with impaired insight

questions.ask: Any problems with your memory?
questions.why: Progressive memory loss with functional decline in an older adult raises dementia; get a collateral history, since patients often underreport it.
points: Progressive memory loss + functional decline in the elderly → dementia (get collateral history)

followups.q: Is it more that you forget recent things, or old memories too?
followups.probes: Recent memory loss with preserved distant memory is the typical early pattern of most dementias

followups.q: Is it affecting daily activities — finances, medications, driving?
followups.probes: Functional decline alongside memory loss is what separates dementia from benign age-related forgetfulness

followups.q: Has anyone else noticed a change, and how has it progressed?
followups.probes: Collateral history is essential — patients with dementia often underreport their own memory loss

questions.ask: Any trouble finding words, or getting words out clearly?
questions.why: Dysphasia (word-finding/language) localises to the dominant hemisphere; dysarthria (slurred articulation) localises to the cerebellum, bulbar muscles or their nerve supply — the distinction matters for localisation.
points: Sudden word-finding difficulty or slurred speech → stroke/TIA until excluded
Gradual word-finding difficulty in an older adult → consider primary progressive aphasia / early dementia

followups.q: Did this come on suddenly, or has it developed gradually?
followups.probes: Sudden → stroke/TIA until excluded; gradual in an older adult → consider primary progressive aphasia or early dementia

followups.q: Is it that you can't find the right words, or that the words come out slurred?
followups.probes: Word-finding difficulty (dysphasia) localises to the dominant hemisphere; slurred articulation (dysarthria) localises to the cerebellum, bulbar muscles, or their nerve supply

followups.q: Any weakness, numbness, or facial droop alongside it?
followups.probes: Any accompanying focal deficit strengthens a stroke/TIA localisation

questions.ask: Any change in your vision, or a curtain/shadow across it?
questions.why: Sudden painless monocular loss in the amaurosis fugax pattern is a TIA warning — cross-reference the ENT & Eyes visual-loss entry for the full differential.
points: Sudden painless monocular visual loss ("curtain") → amaurosis fugax / retinal artery occlusion — a TIA warning

followups.q: Did it come on suddenly, like a curtain coming down over one eye?
followups.probes: Sudden painless monocular visual loss in this pattern is amaurosis fugax — a TIA warning

followups.q: Was it one eye, or both? Has it come back, or is it still there?
followups.probes: Monocular points to the eye or optic nerve; transient and resolved is the classic TIA-warning pattern

questions.ask: Any change in your hearing?
questions.why: New unilateral hearing loss with other cranial nerve signs raises a cerebellopontine angle lesion — cross-reference the ENT & Eyes hearing-loss entry.
points: Unilateral hearing loss + facial numbness/weakness or ataxia → consider a cerebellopontine angle lesion (e.g. acoustic neuroma)

followups.q: Is it one side or both, and did it come on suddenly or gradually?
followups.probes: Sudden unilateral hearing loss is an otological emergency in its own right; gradual unilateral loss raises a cerebellopontine angle lesion

followups.q: Any facial numbness, weakness, or unsteadiness alongside it?
followups.probes: Combined with other cranial nerve signs or ataxia, consider a cerebellopontine angle lesion (e.g. acoustic neuroma)

questions.ask: Any change in your sense of smell?
questions.why: Isolated anosmia can be an early non-motor feature of Parkinson's disease, or reflect a frontal skull-base lesion pressing on the olfactory tract.
points: Isolated anosmia, older adult, no nasal cause → consider a neurodegenerative cause

followups.q: Is it just smell, or has your sense of taste changed too? Any nasal congestion or history of head injury?
followups.probes: Excludes the common local causes (rhinosinusitis, prior head trauma) before considering a neurodegenerative cause

questions.ask: Any weakness or drooping of the face?
questions.why: Sparing of the forehead localises an upper motor neuron (central, e.g. stroke) lesion; forehead involvement means a lower motor neuron (peripheral) lesion — the single most useful localiser in facial weakness.
points: Forehead spared, lower face only → UMN (stroke) — usually with other focal signs
Whole side of the face including the forehead → LMN (Bell's palsy; exclude Ramsay Hunt or a parotid tumour)
questions.red: Sudden facial weakness with other focal neuro signs → stroke until excluded.

followups.q: Can you raise your eyebrows and close your eyes tightly on both sides?
followups.probes: Forehead spared (can still raise eyebrows) → UMN pattern (stroke); whole side including the forehead → LMN pattern (Bell's palsy)

followups.q: Did it come on suddenly, with any other weakness or speech trouble?
followups.probes: Sudden facial weakness with other focal signs → stroke until excluded

followups.q: Any ear pain, rash near the ear, or a lump in front of the ear?
followups.probes: Ear pain/vesicular rash → Ramsay Hunt syndrome; a parotid lump → tumour infiltrating the nerve, not Bell's palsy

questions.ask: Any double vision?
questions.why: Diplopia localises a cranial nerve palsy (III, IV, VI) — think microvascular, compressive (aneurysm), or raised ICP.
points: → cranial nerve palsy (III, IV, VI) — microvascular, compressive (aneurysm), or raised ICP
questions.red: Painful third nerve palsy with a fixed dilated pupil → compressive aneurysm, a neurosurgical emergency.

followups.q: Is the double vision side-by-side, or up-and-down? Does it go away if you cover one eye?
followups.probes: Resolves with one eye covered → true binocular diplopia from a cranial nerve palsy (III, IV, VI), not an ocular/refractive problem

followups.q: Any eyelid droop, or is one pupil bigger than the other? Any pain?
followups.probes: Painful third nerve palsy with a dilated pupil → compressive aneurysm, a neurosurgical emergency

followups.q: Did it come on suddenly, and do you have diabetes or vascular risk factors?
followups.probes: Sudden onset with vascular risk factors supports a microvascular (diabetic) cause — usually pupil-sparing, unlike a compressive lesion

questions.ask: Any weakness in the arms or legs — one side or both? Sudden or gradual?
questions.why: Distribution + tempo localise the lesion along the neuraxis.
points: Sudden, one-sided (face/arm/leg) ± speech → stroke/TIA — a time-critical red flag
Ascending symmetrical weakness over days ± after infection → Guillain–Barré
Proximal, symmetrical, gradual (difficulty with stairs/rising/hair) → myopathy
Weakness worse with use, better with rest, ± ptosis/diplopia → myasthenia
questions.red: Weakness + a sensory level + bladder involvement → cord compression.

followups.q: How quickly did it come on — seconds, over days, or gradually over months?
followups.probes: Sudden (seconds–minutes) → vascular (stroke/TIA) · subacute (days) → inflammatory/infective (Guillain–Barré, myasthenia) · gradual (months) → myopathy or a compressive lesion

followups.q: Is it one side of the body, or both? Does it involve the face as well?
followups.probes: One-sided face/arm/leg → stroke/TIA — a time-critical red flag

followups.q: Has it improved, or is it still there?
followups.probes: Resolution within 24 hours → TIA; persisting beyond that → stroke, with imaging changes to match

followups.q: Any trouble with speech or swallowing alongside it?
followups.probes: Cortical/brainstem involvement — reinforces a stroke localisation

followups.q: Is it worse with repeated use through the day, with drooping eyelids or double vision?
followups.probes: Fatigable weakness plus ptosis/diplopia → myasthenia gravis

followups.q: Any pins and needles, back pain, or bladder/bowel symptoms with it?
followups.probes: Weakness + a sensory level + bladder involvement → cord compression, a surgical emergency

followups.q: Do you have high blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes, atrial fibrillation, or a smoking history?
followups.probes: Sets the pre-test probability for a vascular cause and shapes secondary prevention

followups.q: Are you on blood thinners, or do you have a history of a heart valve problem or fevers?
followups.probes: Anticoagulation changes the bleed-vs-clot calculus; endocarditis is an embolic source worth excluding

questions.ask: Any numbness, pins and needles or altered sensation? Where?
questions.why: The distribution maps the lesion (nerve, root, cord, or brain).
points: Single nerve territory → mononeuropathy/entrapment (e.g. median → carpal tunnel)
A sensory level on the trunk → spinal cord lesion — red flag

followups.q: Where exactly do you feel it — can you show me the boundary?
followups.probes: Distribution maps the lesion: glove-and-stocking → peripheral neuropathy · a single nerve territory → entrapment · a dermatomal band → nerve root · a level on the trunk → spinal cord

followups.q: Did it come on suddenly, with any weakness alongside it?
followups.probes: Sudden, one-sided, with weakness → stroke

followups.q: Is it worse at night, and does shaking your hand or hanging your arm off the bed help?
followups.probes: Nocturnal worsening relieved by shaking the hand (the flick sign) is classic for carpal tunnel/median nerve entrapment

followups.q: Do you have diabetes, drink alcohol, or have any nutritional deficiencies?
followups.probes: The common causes of a symmetrical peripheral neuropathy

questions.ask: Any problems with balance, coordination, or walking? Any falls?
questions.why: Screens the cerebellum, proprioception and the motor system as an integrated output; falls are a major morbidity in the elderly.
points: Broad-based, clumsy, worse in the dark improving with vision → sensory ataxia (proprioceptive)
Broad-based with slurred speech/tremor, not helped by vision → cerebellar
Shuffling, small steps, stooped, reduced arm swing → parkinsonism

followups.q: Is it worse in the dark, or when you close your eyes — like in the shower?
followups.probes: Worse without visual input → sensory (proprioceptive) ataxia; unaffected by vision → cerebellar

followups.q: Any slurred speech, tremor, or clumsiness with your hands as well?
followups.probes: Adds cerebellar signs to the picture, rather than a purely proprioceptive or peripheral one

followups.q: Are your steps small and shuffling, and do your arms swing normally when you walk?
followups.probes: Shuffling, stooped, reduced arm swing → parkinsonism

followups.q: Do you find yourself lifting your foot higher than normal, or tripping on your toes?
followups.probes: A high-stepping gait to clear a dropped foot → peripheral nerve (e.g. common peroneal palsy, peripheral neuropathy)

followups.q: How many falls, and were you injured? What were you doing each time?
followups.probes: Circumstances and injury pattern separate a mechanical/gait problem from a blackout — falls are a major cause of morbidity in the elderly and worth quantifying

questions.ask: Any new problems with bladder or bowel control?
questions.why: New sphincter disturbance with leg symptoms is a spinal-cord red flag — a small question that catches a surgical emergency.
points: Sphincter disturbance (new urinary retention/incontinence or bowel incontinence) + bilateral leg symptoms + saddle numbness → cauda equina / cord compression
Isolated urge/stress incontinence → see GU (usually not neurological)
questions.red: Sphincter disturbance + saddle anaesthesia + bilateral leg weakness → cauda equina — urgent.

followups.q: Is this new, and does it affect your bladder, your bowels, or both?
followups.probes: New sphincter disturbance, especially combined, is what raises concern — long-standing stress incontinence is a different, usually non-neurological, problem

followups.q: Any numbness around your bottom or inner thighs — like sitting on a saddle?
followups.probes: Saddle anaesthesia + sphincter disturbance + leg weakness → cauda equina syndrome, a surgical emergency

followups.q: Any weakness or numbness in the legs alongside it?
followups.probes: Bilateral leg symptoms with sphincter change points to the cord/cauda equina rather than an isolated urological cause

followups.q: Any back pain that came before this?
followups.probes: A preceding disc-type back pain supports a compressive cause at the cord or cauda equina level

questions.ask: Have you had any episodes of losing consciousness?
questions.why: The overlap of syncope (cardiovascular) and seizure (neurological) — the history distinguishes them (cross-reference the cardio syncope entry).
points: Aura, lateral tongue-bite, post-ictal confusion/drowsiness → seizure (jerk duration doesn't discriminate: brief clonic jerks occur in convulsive syncope, and prolonged jerking suggests non-epileptic seizures; incontinence and tongue-biting alone are of limited value)
Prodromal nausea/greying vision, triggered by standing/pain, rapid clear recovery → vasovagal syncope
Exertional, no warning → cardiac (see cardio file) — the dangerous one
Always seek a collateral history from a witness — the patient by definition didn't see it
Recurrent episodes with a family history of sudden death or epilepsy → raises an inherited arrhythmia or epilepsy syndrome

followups.q: Did you lose consciousness completely, and for how long?
followups.probes: Confirms true loss of consciousness rather than presyncope or a non-syncopal spell

followups.q: What were you doing right before — standing up quickly, exercising, or passing urine at night?
followups.probes: Standing → postural hypotension · exercise → cardiac outflow obstruction, a dangerous one · micturition at night → micturition syncope

followups.q: Any warning — feeling sick and in a stuffy room, or a strange smell/déjà vu?
followups.probes: Nausea in a stuffy room → vasovagal; a strange smell or déjà vu is an aura, and points to seizure instead

followups.q: Did you bite your tongue, or lose bladder control during it?
followups.probes: Supports seizure, though of limited value alone — these can occur in convulsive syncope too

followups.q: Did anyone see it, and were there jerking movements? Has anyone filmed it?
followups.probes: A witness account or video is often the single most useful piece of evidence — jerking makes seizure more likely but can occur with cardiac syncope too

followups.q: Did you wake up feeling normal, or drowsy and confused?
followups.probes: Normal on waking → cardiac syncope; drowsy/confused → seizure

followups.q: What medications are you on — blood pressure tablets, heart rhythm drugs, or antiepileptics?
followups.probes: Antihypertensives and antiarrhythmics can precipitate the episode itself

followups.q: Has this happened before, and is there a family history of blackouts, sudden death, or epilepsy?
followups.probes: Recurrence pattern and family history shift the differential toward an inherited arrhythmia or epilepsy syndrome

questions.ask: Have you ever had a fit or convulsion?
questions.why: Distinguishes provoked from unprovoked and localises. Ask about aura (focal onset), and precipitants (alcohol withdrawal, sleep deprivation, flashing lights, missed medication).
points: Precipitants: alcohol withdrawal, sleep deprivation, missed medication

followups.q: Can you describe exactly what happened, from the very start?
followups.probes: A detailed blow-by-blow account is more useful than the label "seizure" — establishes focal vs generalised onset

followups.q: Did you get any warning beforehand — an odd smell or taste, déjà vu, or a rising feeling in your chest?
followups.probes: An aura is itself a focal (aware) seizure and localises the onset

followups.q: Were you stiff and jerking, or did you just go blank and stare?
followups.probes: Tonic–clonic movements → generalised or focal-to-bilateral seizure; blank staring with automatisms (picking, lip-smacking) → focal impaired-awareness seizure

followups.q: Did you bite your tongue, or lose bladder control?
followups.probes: Supports a seizure, though of limited value alone

followups.q: How did you feel afterwards — confused, drowsy, or any weakness that took a while to settle?
followups.probes: Post-ictal drowsiness/confusion supports seizure; transient weakness afterward is Todd's paresis, not a new stroke

followups.q: Any missed medication, heavy alcohol use or a recent stop, lack of sleep, or flashing lights beforehand?
followups.probes: The classic precipitants — worth asking specifically, as patients often don't volunteer them

followups.q: Has this happened before? How often, and is there a pattern — time of day, during sleep?
followups.probes: Recurrence and timing shape the diagnosis of epilepsy versus a single provoked event

followups.q: Is there a family history of epilepsy, or any past head injury, meningitis, or brain scan?
followups.probes: Family history and a structural cause (old injury, past infection) both raise the pre-test probability of a seizure disorder

questions.ask: When you say dizzy, do you mean the room spins, or more light-headed?
questions.why: "Dizziness" splits into two unrelated pathways — force the patient to define it.
points: Room spinning (vertigo) → vestibular: BPPV (brief, positional), vestibular neuritis (acute, sustained), Ménière's (with hearing loss/tinnitus); central causes (brainstem/cerebellar stroke) if with other neuro signs → red flag
Light-headed/faint → presyncope: cardiovascular/orthostatic (back to the cardio pathway)

followups.q: When you say dizzy, do you mean the room is spinning, or more that you feel faint/light-headed?
followups.probes: Forces the split between vertigo (vestibular) and presyncope (cardiovascular) — patients are poor at distinguishing these unprompted

followups.q: Does it happen with a change in head position — rolling over in bed, or looking up?
followups.probes: Brief, positional, seconds to minutes → BPPV

followups.q: How long does each episode last — seconds, hours, or is it constant?
followups.probes: Seconds–minutes and positional → BPPV · hours with hearing loss/tinnitus → Ménière's · persistent over 24h without hearing loss → vestibular neuritis

followups.q: Any hearing loss or ringing in the ears with it?
followups.probes: Present suggests a labyrinthine/cochlear process (labyrinthitis, Ménière's, or rarely a stroke affecting the inner ear); absent favours vestibular neuritis or BPPV

followups.q: Any double vision, slurred speech, weakness, or clumsiness alongside it?
followups.probes: Any of these with vertigo points to a central (brainstem/cerebellar) cause — a red flag, not simple peripheral vertigo

followups.q: Can you still stand and walk during an episode, or does it stop you completely?
followups.probes: Able to walk, though unsteady → peripheral; unable to stand or walk at all → more suggestive of a central cause

followups.q: Any nausea, vomiting, sweating, or headache with it?
followups.probes: Common with severe vertigo of either origin, but headache alongside neuro signs raises central causes

followups.q: Is it only present on standing, or does it happen at rest too?
followups.probes: Only on standing → presyncope/orthostatic — back to the cardiovascular pathway, not a primary vestibular problem

questions.ask: Do you get headaches? Tell me about them.
questions.why: Overwhelmingly benign (tension, migraine) but hosts several neurological emergencies — the whole skill is pattern-matching the dangerous ones.
points: Thunderclap — instant, worst-ever, "hit on the head" → subarachnoid haemorrhage until excluded
Headache + fever + neck stiffness + photophobia ± rash → meningitis
Worse in the morning / on coughing/bending, with vomiting → raised intracranial pressure (mass)
New headache >50 with scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, visual loss → giant cell arteritis
Unilateral, throbbing, with aura/nausea/photophobia, recurrent → migraine
Bouts over weeks, strictly unilateral around one eye, with watering/red eye, nose running, restless and pacing → cluster headache (the "alarm clock" headache — wakes them at the same time each night)
questions.red: SNOOP: Systemic (fever, weight loss), Neuro deficit, Onset sudden, Older (>50 new), Papilloedema/positional/pattern change.

followups.q: Was it at its worst in the very first second — like being hit on the head?
followups.probes: Thunderclap onset → subarachnoid haemorrhage. It's the speed to maximum that flags it, not the severity

followups.q: Any fever, or does it hurt to bend your neck forward?
followups.probes: Fever + neck stiffness + photophobia → meningitis

followups.q: Is it worse first thing in the morning, or when you cough or bend forward? Any vomiting?
followups.probes: Worse on waking or with Valsalva → raised intracranial pressure

followups.q: Is your scalp tender brushing your hair? Does your jaw ache when you chew?
followups.probes: Giant cell arteritis — ask this of anyone over 50 with a new headache

followups.q: Any weakness, numbness, or trouble with speech or vision alongside it?
followups.probes: Any focal deficit → structural or vascular cause, not a primary headache

followups.q: How long does each one last, and how often do you get them?
followups.probes: Seconds → neuralgia · 15–180 min in bouts → cluster · 4–72 h → migraine · daily and constant → tension-type or medication-overuse

followups.q: Any warning before it starts — flashing lights or zigzag lines? Does light bother you?
followups.probes: Aura and photophobia → migraine

followups.q: How often are you taking painkillers for it?
followups.probes: Most days → medication-overuse headache — common, missed, reversible

systems.drill: BRAIN: confusion/delirium, memory, speech · CRANIAL: vision, hearing, smell, facial weakness, diplopia · CORD/NERVE: weakness (sudden vs gradual), numbness/tingling (distribution), coordination/balance/gait, falls · EPISODES: blackouts, seizures, dizziness (vertigo vs faint) · HEAD: headache (SOCRATES + SNOOP red flags)
systems.seeAlso: Psychiatric — cognition, delirium and dementia overlap; ENT & Eyes — vision and vertigo

systems.name: Musculoskeletal / Rheum
systems.scaffoldIntro: Ask what the joints/muscles are doing wrong, then whether it's systemic:

chunks.gen: Activities of daily living, grip, walking
Rash, eyes, Raynaud's, mouth ulcers, fatigue

systems.scaffoldOutro: The master discriminator is **inflammatory vs mechanical**, and one question does most of the work: **duration of early-morning stiffness** (≥1 hour = classic RA / peripheral inflammatory; ≥30 min in the axial/spondyloarthritis context; <30 min or "after rest" = mechanical/OA). The pattern of joint involvement (which joints, symmetry, number) does the rest.

questions.ask: Which joints are painful? Sudden or gradual? Does it move around? Any injury?
questions.why: The pattern — number of joints, symmetry, distribution, and tempo — is the core of rheumatological diagnosis.
points: Symmetrical small joints (MCPs, PIPs, wrists), gradual → rheumatoid arthritis
DIPs/PIPs and thumb base, often symmetrical (primary nodal OA — Heberden's/Bouchard's), or asymmetrical large weight-bearing joints (secondary OA), pain worse with use → osteoarthritis
Single hot joint, acute, exquisite, first MTP → gout (or, until excluded, septic arthritis — a red flag)
Migratory large-joint pain → rheumatic fever, gonococcal, reactive
Axial (spine/sacroiliac) in a young adult with inflammatory pattern → ankylosing spondylitis
questions.red: A single acutely hot, swollen, painful joint is septic arthritis until proven otherwise — needs aspiration, not reassurance.

questions.ask: Any back pain? Anything make it worse? Does it go down your legs?
questions.why: Mostly mechanical, but hosts several red-flag conditions; the pattern and associated features triage it.
points: Worse with activity, better with rest, no systemic features → mechanical
Inflammatory back pain: young adult, insidious, worse in the morning/at rest, better with exercise, night pain → spondyloarthritis
Radiating below the knee + dermatomal numbness/weakness → radiculopathy (disc)
questions.red: Bladder/bowel dysfunction + saddle anaesthesia (cauda equina), thoracic pain, fever/IVDU (discitis/abscess), weight loss/history of cancer (metastasis), age <20 or >55 new onset, trauma/osteoporosis (fracture).

questions.ask: Are your joints stiff in the morning? How long before they loosen?
questions.why: The best single discriminator of inflammatory vs mechanical disease.
points: Prolonged morning stiffness — ≥1 hour for classic RA (≥30 min in axial spondyloarthritis), easing with activity → inflammatory (RA, spondyloarthritis). Note morning stiffness is a supportive clue, not a scored ACR/EULAR criterion
Brief stiffness (<30 min) or stiffness after rest/activity, worse through the day → mechanical/OA
Proximal (shoulder/hip girdle) stiffness in someone >50 + raised inflammatory markers → polymyalgia rheumatica (ask about GCA symptoms)

questions.ask: Are the joints swollen? Warm or red?
questions.why: Confirms synovitis (soft, boggy swelling) vs bony enlargement (OA) vs effusion, and warmth/redness raises infection/crystal disease.
points: Soft symmetrical swelling of small joints → inflammatory synovitis (RA)
Hard, bony swellings at DIPs (Heberden's) → OA
Single hot red swollen joint → gout/pseudogout/sepsis

questions.ask: What can't you do now that you could before — dressing, gripping, stairs?
questions.why: Rheumatology is a functional specialty; disability drives management and reveals severity better than pain scores.

questions.ask: Any visible deformity, or joints giving way / feeling unstable?
questions.why: Deformity and instability signal structural joint damage — chronic erosive disease or ligamentous injury — rather than active inflammation alone.

questions.ask: Any skin rashes, mouth ulcers, or dry/red eyes?
questions.why: Extra-articular skin and mucosal clues point to a specific connective tissue disease and separate it from isolated joint disease.
points: Photosensitive malar rash + mouth ulcers + arthralgia → SLE
Arthritis + diarrhoea/bloody stool or eye inflammation → enteropathic/reactive (the seronegative spectrum)

questions.ask: Do your fingers change colour in the cold? Any hair loss or persistent fatigue?
questions.why: Raynaud's (white→blue→red) with rash/arthralgia points to SLE, systemic sclerosis or mixed CTD; hair loss and fatigue are non-specific but common accompaniments of active CTD.
points: Raynaud's (white→blue→red fingers in cold) + rash/arthralgia → SLE, systemic sclerosis, mixed CTD

systems.drill: PAIN: which joints, pattern (symmetry/number/distribution), tempo, back pain (+ red flags) · STIFFNESS: morning stiffness duration (inflammatory vs mechanical) · SWELLING: swelling/warmth/redness (single hot joint = ?septic) · FUNCTION: ADLs, grip, mobility · SYSTEMIC: rash, eyes, mouth ulcers, Raynaud's, hair loss, fatigue

systems.name: Endocrine
systems.scaffoldIntro: The endocrine screen is best remembered gland-by-gland, because each gland's excess/deficiency has a signature. Run down the axis:

chunks.gen: Heat/cold intolerance, weight, bowels, tremor, neck swelling, palpitations

systems.scaffoldOutro: The unifying trick: most endocrine disease is a **too-much / too-little pair** with mirror-image symptoms. Learn one side and the other is its opposite — the mirror tables below are the fastest way to hold hyper vs hypo in your head.

questions.ask: Do you feel the heat or cold more than others? Change in weight, bowels, mood, energy? Any neck swelling or trouble breathing/swallowing?
questions.why: Thyroid hormone sets the metabolic rate, so its excess/deficiency touches nearly every system. Screening the paired cluster is more sensitive than any single symptom — and because the two states mirror each other, the pattern itself is the diagnosis.

rows: Dry skin, hair changes, hoarse voice

points: A visible/palpable neck lump moving on swallowing → screen obstructive symptoms (shortness of breath, wheeze, stridor, dysphagia, voice change) and malignancy features (rapid growth, fixed lump, lymph nodes)

questions.ask: Are you passing a lot of urine and drinking more than usual? Any unexplained weight loss or blurred vision?
questions.why: The osmotic symptoms of hyperglycaemia are the classic presentation; the acute end (ketosis) is a red flag.
points: Recurrent infections (thrush, skin, urinary) and slow healing
questions.red: Rapid-onset ketotic symptoms → type 1 / DKA — an emergency.

questions.ask: Do you ever go shaky, sweaty or confused, relieved by eating?
questions.why: Only relevant if the patient is on insulin or a sulfonylurea — otherwise you can usually skip it. Where relevant, it drives safety and treatment adjustment.
points: Neuroglycopenic: morning headaches, confusion, disturbance of conscious state, seizures
Not on insulin or a sulfonylurea → hypoglycaemia unlikely, can skip

questions.ask: Has the diabetes affected your eyes, kidneys, nerves, feet or heart?
questions.why: Long-term hyperglycaemia damages small and large vessels — screening the end-organs is core to every established-diabetes review.
points: Microvascular: visual disturbance (retinopathy), renal dysfunction, peripheral neuropathy (numbness, foot ulcers)
Macrovascular: heart disease, peripheral vascular disease, stroke
Other: erectile dysfunction (early vascular + autonomic marker), non-healing ulcers

questions.ask: When were you diagnosed? How is it managed? How well controlled is it? Any complications?
questions.why: For an established chronic disease you switch from screening to characterising. This four-part frame — timeframe → management → current control → complications — is a template you can reuse for almost any known chronic condition (asthma, IHD, IBD).
points: Timeframe: when diagnosed, type 1 vs type 2
Management: diet, oral agents, insulin (regimen), who monitors it
Current control: HbA1c if known, home glucose readings, frequency of hypos, recent admissions

questions.ask: Persistent fatigue, dizziness on standing, or skin darkening? Or the opposite — central weight gain, easy bruising, purple stretch marks?
questions.why: Rare but dangerous and easily missed; cortisol excess and deficiency look completely different. Ask about steroid use first — exogenous steroids are by far the commonest cause of Cushing's.
points: Ask about steroid use — the commonest cause of Cushing's
questions.red: Addisonian crisis (hypotension, collapse) is an emergency.

questions.ask: Any headaches, or a change in your side (peripheral) vision?
questions.why: A pituitary mass presses upward on the optic chiasm, classically producing bitemporal hemianopia — a mass effect independent of which hormone is over- or under-produced.

questions.ask: Have your hands, feet or facial features changed — bigger rings, shoe size, jaw?
questions.why: Excess growth hormone after epiphyseal closure thickens soft tissue and bone rather than causing height growth — the change is usually gradual enough that old photos are more revealing than the patient's own recollection.
points: Enlarging hands/feet (ring/shoe size), coarse features, sweating → acromegaly

questions.ask: Any milk discharge from the breasts?
questions.why: Prolactin excess suppresses the gonadal axis, so galactorrhoea usually travels with amenorrhoea or low libido rather than appearing alone.

questions.ask: Any kidney stones, bone pain, tummy pains, constipation, low mood — or tingling and muscle cramps?
questions.why: Hypercalcaemia has a neat mnemonic — "stones, bones, abdominal groans, psychiatric moans" — and hypocalcaemia is the neuromuscular mirror.
points: Hypercalcaemia → primary hyperparathyroidism or malignancy (pair with the weight-loss/cancer screen)
Hypocalcaemia → post-thyroid/parathyroid surgery, vitamin D deficiency, CKD

questions.ask: Change in libido, sexual function or periods? Hot flushes? Change in body or facial hair?
questions.why: Sex-steroid axes overlap with thyroid, pituitary and adrenal disease; changes here often surface an endocrine cause. (For the full reproductive and sexual history, see the Reproductive system file.)
points: Hot flushes + irregular then absent periods → menopause
Low libido + fatigue + loss of body hair → hypogonadism

items: Skin: sweaty + tremor | dry + hoarse voice
Hyperglycaemia: polyuria, polydipsia, nocturia, blurred vision, weight loss
Hypoglycaemia (if on insulin): tremor, sweating, confusion, morning headache
Complications: eyes, renal, neuropathy, feet, heart, ED
Known diabetes: timeframe / management / current control / complications
Cushing: central obesity, striae, bruising, proximal weakness
Addison: fatigue, postural dizziness, pigmentation, salt craving
Hyper: stones, bones, abdominal groans, psychiatric moans

systems.drill: THYROID: hyper|hypo mirror (weight, temperature, bowels, cardiac, menstrual, skin) + goitre/obstructive · GLUCOSE: hyperglycaemia symptoms, hypoglycaemia (if on insulin), complications, known-diabetes frame (timeframe/management/control/complications) · ADRENAL: Cushing|Addison mirror (steroid use?) · PITUITARY: headache/visual fields, acral growth, galactorrhoea · CALCIUM: hyper|hypo mirror (stones/bones/groans/moans vs tingling/tetany) · GONADAL: libido, menses, hirsutism. Most endocrine disease is a too-much/too-little pair.
systems.seeAlso: Reproductive & Sexual History — the gonadal axis and menstrual/sexual symptoms

systems.name: Haematological
systems.scaffoldIntro: Blood has three jobs — carry oxygen, fight infection, and clot. Disease is failure of one of the three, plus the reticuloendothelial signs:

chunks.gen: Lumps (lymphadenopathy), abdominal fullness (spleen), night sweats, weight loss, itch, bone pain

systems.scaffoldOutro: Haematology overlaps heavily with the **constitutional screen** (B symptoms) — the two are best learned together. A failure of *all three* cell lines (anaemia + bleeding + infections) points to marrow failure.

questions.ask: Do you feel tired, breathless on exertion, or dizzy on standing? Have people said you look pale?
questions.why: Anaemia reduces oxygen delivery, producing a predictable symptom cluster; the job then is to find why (blood loss, deficiency, haemolysis, marrow).
points: Fatigue + exertional dyspnoea + pallor ± palpitations, postural dizziness → anaemia; then hunt the cause:

Ask about blood loss: heavy periods (women — the commonest cause of iron deficiency), GI bleeding (melaena, PR blood), and the change-in-bowel-habit/weight-loss cancer screen (right-sided colon cancer classically presents as iron-deficiency anaemia)
Diet (vegan → B12), pica and restless legs (iron deficiency), jaundice (haemolysis)
Ask about GI symptoms of malabsorption (coeliac) and known chronic disease (renal, inflammatory)
questions.red: Iron-deficiency anaemia in a man or postmenopausal woman is a GI cancer until excluded.

questions.ask: Any mouth ulcers?
questions.why: Recurrent or severe mouth ulcers can be a mucosal bleeding-tendency sign, or reflect the neutropenia of marrow failure — worth asking separately rather than folding into 'bruising'.
points: Isolated, recurrent, no other bleeding/infection signs → usually benign aphthous ulcers

questions.ask: Do you bruise easily or bleed more than expected — gums, nosebleeds, after cuts? Blood in urine or stool?
questions.why: The pattern of bleeding separates platelet/vascular from coagulation-factor disease — see the discriminator table below.
points: Mucocutaneous bleeding — petechiae, purpura, gum/nose bleeding, menorrhagia → platelet problem (thrombocytopenia, e.g. ITP; or dysfunction)
Deep bleeding — into joints/muscles, delayed bleeding after trauma → coagulation factor problem (haemophilia, warfarin, DIC, liver disease)
Ask about anticoagulants/antiplatelets and family history of bleeding
questions.red: New widespread bruising + fatigue + infections → marrow failure/leukaemia.

questions.ask: Ever had a clot in the leg or lung? Any leg swelling or pain? Recent flights, surgery or immobility?
questions.why: The clotting system can also over-perform. Screens for VTE and thrombophilia, and connects to the constitutional/malignancy screen (cancer is prothrombotic).
points: Unilateral calf swelling/pain → DVT; with pleuritic pain/dyspnoea → PE
Recurrent or unprovoked VTE, or in unusual sites, or family history → thrombophilia; also an occult-cancer trigger
Ask about provoking factors: surgery, immobility, long flights, oestrogens, pregnancy

questions.ask: Do you get frequent, severe or unusual infections that take a long time to clear?
questions.why: Screens white-cell number/function and immune competence. Recurrent severe infection can be the presentation of leukaemia, marrow failure, or immunodeficiency.
points: Frequent severe bacterial infections + fatigue + bruising → marrow failure/leukaemia
Recurrent infections + weight loss + risk factors → HIV — ask sensitively about risk
Recurrent specific infection types can point to specific immune defects

questions.ask: Any lumps in the neck, armpits or groin?
questions.why: Painless, rubbery, persistent nodes with B symptoms are the hallmark of lymphoma; tender nodes with a recent infection are usually reactive.
points: Painless rubbery persistent nodes + drenching night sweats + weight loss + itch → lymphoma (the B-symptom cluster)
Tender, associated with a local infection → reactive

questions.ask: Any fullness or discomfort in the upper-left abdomen, or filling up quickly when you eat?
questions.why: The spleen enlarges quietly — early satiety from it pressing on the stomach is often the only clue before it's felt on examination.
points: Left-upper-quadrant fullness/early satiety → splenomegaly (myeloproliferative disease, lymphoma, haemolysis)

questions.ask: Any night sweats, weight loss, or generalised itching?
questions.why: This triad — the classic 'B symptoms' — marks lymphoproliferative and myeloproliferative disease as systemic, not just a nodal or marrow problem; itch after a hot shower with a ruddy complexion specifically suggests polycythaemia.
points: Drenching night sweats + weight loss + itch → the B-symptom cluster (lymphoma)
Generalised itch (esp. after a hot shower) + ruddy complexion → polycythaemia

questions.ask: Any persistent bone pain?
questions.why: Marrow infiltration or expansion causes bone pain directly — in an older patient with fatigue and recurrent infection it raises myeloma.
points: Bone pain + fatigue + recurrent infection + thirst/constipation (hypercalcaemia) in an older patient → myeloma

items: Find the cause: blood loss? diet? haemolysis?

systems.drill: CARRY: fatigue, exertional dyspnoea, pallor, dizziness — then find the cause (blood loss? diet? haemolysis?) · CLOT: easy bruising/bleeding (mucocutaneous vs deep), anticoagulants; thrombosis (DVT/PE, provokers) · FIGHT: recurrent/severe/unusual infections · NODES/ORGANS: lymphadenopathy, splenic fullness, night sweats, weight loss, itch, bone pain

discriminator.title: platelet/vascular vs coagulation-factor bleeding
rows: Skin & mucosa (petechiae, purpura, gums, epistaxis, menorrhagia)

systems.seeAlso: General / Constitutional — the B-symptom screen (weight loss, fever, night sweats)

systems.name: Skin (Dermatological)
systems.scaffoldIntro: For any skin complaint, characterise the lesion, then ask what it's doing and what it signals:

chunks.gen: New rash/lesion — where, what does it look like, distribution
Changing size/shape/colour of a mole; non-healing
New drugs, contacts, sun, occupation, travel

systems.scaffoldOutro: Two red-flag threads: the **changing/non-healing lesion** (skin cancer / melanoma) and the **rash-plus-systemic-upset** (drug reaction, vasculitis, meningococcaemia, connective-tissue disease).

questions.ask: Tell me about the rash — where did it start, where is it now, what does it look like?
questions.why: Distribution and morphology are the whole diagnosis in dermatology. Extensor vs flexor, symmetrical vs localised, and dermatomal patterns each point somewhere specific.
points: Symmetrical, extensor surfaces, well-demarcated scaly plaques → psoriasis (ask about nails, joints, scalp)
Flexural, itchy, in an atopic person → eczema/atopic dermatitis
Dermatomal, unilateral, painful vesicles not crossing the midline → shingles (herpes zoster)
A single well-defined patch matching contact with something → contact dermatitis

questions.ask: Is it itchy, painful, weeping or bleeding?
questions.why: These qualities narrow the differential and gauge severity.
points: Intensely itchy → eczema, urticaria, scabies (worse at night, burrows, contacts affected), dermatitis herpetiformis
Bleeding/crusting/non-healing → suspicious for skin malignancy (see below)

questions.ask: Have any moles or spots changed in size, shape or colour?
questions.why: Melanoma is caught by change — the ABCDE rule structures what to ask about.
points: Changing mole — use ABCDE (Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Colour variation, Diameter >6 mm, Evolving) → melanoma until excluded
questions.red: A new or changing pigmented lesion — never file under reassurance without looking.

questions.ask: Anything on your skin that won't heal?
questions.why: Keratinocyte cancers present as non-healing rather than as change — a lesion sitting there for months on sun-exposed skin is the tell.
points: Pearly nodule with telangiectasia / rolled edge, slowly growing, sun-exposed site → basal cell carcinoma
Scaly/crusted or ulcerated non-healing lesion on sun-exposed skin → squamous cell carcinoma
Any non-healing lesion >4–6 weeks → needs examination

questions.ask: Any fever, joint pains, mouth or genital ulcers, or feeling generally unwell with the rash?
questions.why: Skin is a window on internal disease; a rash with systemic upset changes the whole differential toward the dangerous.
points: Non-blanching purpuric rash + fever + unwell → meningococcaemia / vasculitis — emergency red flag (do the glass/tumbler test)
Rash + mucosal involvement + skin peeling + new drug → Stevens–Johnson / TEN — dermatological emergency
Photosensitive facial rash + joint pain + mouth ulcers + hair loss → SLE
Rash + joint pain + gut symptoms → the connective-tissue / reactive spectrum (cross-reference MSK)
questions.red: Non-blanching purpuric rash + fever is an emergency — do the glass test.

questions.ask: Started any new medications, creams or products? Any new contacts, sun, occupation or travel?
questions.why: So much of dermatology is external cause — drugs and contacts especially. A new drug within days–weeks of a rash is a drug eruption until proven otherwise.
points: New drug + widespread symmetrical rash → drug eruption (ask specifically — patients forget antibiotics)
New topical/occupational contactant + localised rash → contact dermatitis
Sun exposure + rash on exposed sites → photosensitivity (idiopathic or drug-induced)

systems.drill: LESION: site of onset & spread, morphology, distribution (extensor/flexor/dermatomal) · SYMPTOMS: itch, pain, weeping, bleeding · CHANGE: changing mole (ABCDE), non-healing lesion · SYSTEMIC: fever, joints, mucosal ulcers, unwell (non-blanching rash = emergency) · EXPOSURE: new drugs, contacts, sun, occupation, travel

systems.name: Psychiatric
systems.scaffold: MOOD → ANXIETY → PSYCHOSIS → COGNITION → SUBSTANCES → RISK
systems.scaffoldIntro: The psychiatric screen samples mood, thought, perception and risk. Remember it as a descent from the common to the critical, always ending on risk:

chunks.gen: Low mood, anhedonia, sleep, appetite, energy, guilt; elevated mood/overactivity
Self-harm, suicide, risk to others, self-neglect

systems.scaffoldOutro: **Risk is never optional and always last-but-not-least.** The golden rule: asking about suicide does not plant the idea — it is a required, protective part of the screen. Two mnemonics do the heavy lifting: **SIGECAPS** for depression and **CAGE** for alcohol.

questions.ask: How has your mood been? Do you still enjoy the things you used to?
questions.why: Low mood plus anhedonia are the two core features; the SIGECAPS cluster establishes whether threshold criteria are met and gauges severity.
points: Low mood or anhedonia (at least one of the two core features required) + a total of ≥5 SIGECAPS symptoms for ≥2 weeks → major depression

Screen for organic mimics: hypothyroidism, Parkinson's disease, chronic illness (e.g. HIV, heart failure), and drugs (interferons, chemotherapy) — depression still deserves a physical differential (the beta-blocker–depression link is contested; anaemia mimics the fatigue presentation rather than depression itself)
Low mood + chronic pain/illness → reactive/adjustment vs comorbid depression
SIGECAPS = Sleep, Interest (anhedonia), Guilt/worthlessness, Energy, Concentration, Appetite/weight, Psychomotor change, Suicidality

questions.ask: Any times you felt unusually high, energetic, needing little sleep, doing risky things?
questions.why: You cannot diagnose depression safely without screening for bipolarity — antidepressants can precipitate mania, and a missed manic history changes management entirely.
points: Elevated/irritable mood + reduced need for sleep + grandiosity + overspending/risk-taking + pressured speech, sustained days → manic episode (bipolar)
Distinguish from the sustained overactivity of stimulant use or hyperthyroidism

questions.ask: Do you worry a lot, more days than not?
questions.why: Persistent, hard-to-control worry across multiple areas of life, with physical tension, is generalised anxiety disorder — common and frequently somatised.
points: Persistent excessive worry most days, with restlessness/tension/poor sleep → generalised anxiety

questions.ask: Do you get sudden attacks of intense fear with physical symptoms, out of the blue?
questions.why: Panic disorder is a real and common diagnosis, but it's also a diagnosis of exclusion in the moment — the physical symptoms overlap completely with cardiac, respiratory and endocrine emergencies.
points: Discrete attacks of terror with palpitations, chest tightness, paraesthesiae, fear of dying → panic disorder — but exclude hyperthyroidism, phaeochromocytoma, arrhythmia/MI and PE first

questions.ask: Any repetitive thoughts that keep intruding, or rituals you feel you have to do?
questions.why: OCD is defined by the pairing — intrusive thoughts causing distress, and compulsions performed to relieve that distress — not by either alone.
points: Intrusive thoughts + compulsive rituals to relieve them → OCD

questions.ask: Has anything very frightening or traumatic happened to you? Do you get flashbacks or avoid things that remind you of it?
questions.why: PTSD requires a specific link to trauma exposure, distinguishing it from anxiety that arises without a triggering event.
points: Anxiety tied to a specific trauma with flashbacks/avoidance/hypervigilance → PTSD

questions.ask: Ever heard or seen things others couldn't? Held beliefs others found unusual, or felt your thoughts interfered with?
questions.why: Screens perception and thought. Ask matter-of-factly. First-rank-type symptoms and their tempo help separate primary psychosis, mood-congruent psychosis, and organic/drug-induced causes.
points: Auditory hallucinations (esp. third-person/running commentary) + delusions + thought interference, chronic → schizophrenia spectrum
Psychosis congruent with extreme mood (grandiose in mania, nihilistic in severe depression) → mood disorder with psychotic features
Acute onset with clouded consciousness/fluctuation, visual hallucinations → think delirium/organic or drug-induced — a medical, not primary psychiatric, emergency

questions.ask: Any problems with memory or concentration?
questions.why: Bridges to neurology; distinguishes depression ("pseudodementia"), delirium and dementia — which have very different urgencies. (See the neuro delirium/dementia entry.)

questions.ask: How much alcohol in a typical week? Any recreational drugs?
questions.why: Substance use causes, mimics and complicates every other psychiatric presentation, and withdrawal can be life-threatening. Quantify, and screen for dependence.
points: Positive CAGE (Cut down, Annoyed, Guilty, Eye-opener; ≥2 positive) / high intake + morning drinking + withdrawal (tremor, sweats, seizures) → alcohol dependence (current Australian first-line screening uses AUDIT-C; CAGE is the older, dependence-weighted tool)
Screen for complications: mood, liver, GI bleeding, nutrition, social
Ask about stimulants (can mimic mania/psychosis/panic) and opioids (withdrawal, overdose risk)

questions.ask: Sometimes when people feel this low they have thoughts life isn't worth living, or of harming themselves. Have you had thoughts like that?
questions.why: The single most important part of the psychiatric review. Escalate gently through the stages; a plan, means, and intent mark high risk.
points: Active ideation + plan + means + intent + prior attempts → high acute risk — needs urgent safety action, never send away
Fleeting passive thoughts, no plan/intent, strong protective factors and support → lower acute risk, but document and safety-net
questions.red: Never send away a patient with a plan, means and intent — act on safety.

questions.ask: Any thoughts of harming anyone else? How are you managing day to day — eating, washing, paying bills?
questions.why: Risk assessment isn't only about the patient's own safety — thoughts of harming others and an inability to care for oneself both change the urgency and the disposition.
points: Specific threats or plans toward a named person → duty-to-warn considerations, urgent escalation
Self-neglect (not eating, not managing medications/finances, unsafe living conditions) → vulnerability requiring support, even without active risk

items: Mania screen (elevated mood, reduced sleep need, risk-taking)
Memory, concentration (delirium vs dementia vs depression)
Self-harm / suicide (ideation → plan → means → intent → past attempts)

systems.drill: MOOD: depression (low mood + anhedonia + SIGECAPS), mania screen · ANXIETY: worry, panic, phobias, OCD, PTSD · PSYCHOSIS: hallucinations, delusions, thought interference · COGNITION: memory/concentration (delirium vs dementia vs depression) · SUBSTANCES: alcohol (CAGE + quantity), drugs · RISK: self-harm/suicide (ideation→plan→means→intent→past attempts), risk to others, self-neglect
systems.clnote: Risk is never optional and always assessed — asking about suicide is protective, not suggestive.
systems.seeAlso: Neurological — the delirium / dementia / cognition overlap

systems.name: ENT & Eyes
systems.scaffoldIntro: Two regional screens that often sit at the end of the systems review. Take them organ by organ:

chunks.gen: Hearing loss, tinnitus, discharge, earache, vertigo
Blockage, discharge, epistaxis, smell, facial pain
Sore throat, hoarseness, swallowing, neck lumps
Visual loss, pain, red eye, double vision, discharge

systems.scaffoldOutro: The red-flag threads: **sudden loss** (sudden hearing loss, sudden visual loss = emergencies), **unilateral persistent symptoms** (unilateral hearing loss/nasal obstruction/neck lump → tumour), and **painful red eye** (sight-threatening).

questions.ask: Has your hearing changed — one ear or both? Sudden or gradual?
questions.why: The tempo and laterality triage it — from wax to a treatable emergency to a tumour.
points: Gradual, bilateral, high-frequency, older/noise exposure → presbyacusis/noise-induced (sensorineural)
Sudden sensorineural loss → emergency — needs same-day ENT (treatable window)
Unilateral persistent sensorineural loss ± tinnitus → exclude acoustic neuroma
Conductive loss with blockage/discharge → wax, effusion, perforation, otosclerosis
questions.red: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss has a treatable window — refer same day.

questions.ask: Any ringing or buzzing in the ears? One side or both — constant, or pulsing with your heartbeat?
questions.why: Pulsatile or strictly unilateral tinnitus needs vascular/tumour work-up; most tinnitus tracks with hearing loss or an ototoxic drug (aminoglycosides, loop diuretics, aspirin/NSAIDs, quinine, some chemotherapy agents).
points: Pulsatile or strictly unilateral → needs investigation (vascular anomaly, acoustic neuroma)
Bilateral, non-pulsatile, with noise exposure or an ototoxic drug on the list → benign/drug-related

questions.ask: Any discharge or pain from the ear?
questions.why: Localises within the outer, middle or inner ear and separates simple infection from the sinister chronic discharge of cholesteatoma.
points: Foul, chronic discharge + hearing loss → cholesteatoma — needs ENT referral

questions.ask: Do you get spells where the room feels like it's spinning?
questions.why: True rotational vertigo localises to the vestibular system or its central connections — cross-reference the Neurological Dizziness/vertigo entry for the full vertigo-vs-presyncope work-up.

questions.ask: Is your nose blocked or running? One side or both?
questions.why: Bilateral symptoms are usually allergic or infective; persistent unilateral symptoms need a tumour excluded.
points: Bilateral blockage + sneezing + itch + clear discharge, seasonal → allergic rhinitis
Unilateral blockage or discharge, persistent → exclude nasal/sinus tumour
Foreign body (children) or deviated septum → structural, usually unilateral and longstanding
questions.red: Persistent unilateral nasal obstruction or discharge → tumour until excluded.

questions.ask: Have you ever had nosebleeds? How often, how much, and do they stop easily?
questions.why: Most epistaxis is local (trauma, nose-picking, dry mucosa), but recurrent, severe or bilateral bleeding raises anticoagulant/antiplatelet use, bleeding disorders and, rarely, a nasal tumour.
points: Recurrent, minor, with dry air/nose-picking → local trauma, the commonest cause
On antiplatelets/anticoagulants, or bruising elsewhere → medication effect or a bleeding disorder (haematological malignancy, haemophilia)
Severe enough to need transfusion, or unilateral and persistent in an older adult → exclude nasal tumour
Hypertension is commonly cited as a cause but the causal link is contested — treat it as a soft association, not an established one

questions.ask: Any change in your sense of smell — or taste, since the two often go together?
questions.why: Anosmia localises to mechanical obstruction (polyps), infection (including post-viral/COVID), or trauma if complete; isolated anosmia in an older adult can be an early non-motor feature of neurodegenerative disease.
points: With nasal obstruction or known polyps → local/mechanical
Post-viral (including post-COVID) → common, usually recovers over weeks to months
Isolated, no nasal symptoms, older adult → consider a neurodegenerative cause

questions.ask: Any pain or pressure over your face or sinuses — worse bending forward?
questions.why: Localises inflammation to the paranasal sinuses; pain above the eye points to frontal sinusitis, periorbital pain to ethmoid sinusitis.
points: Facial pain/pressure + purulent nasal discharge + maxillary toothache, worse bending forward, post-URTI → sinusitis
Itchy eyes + sneezing, no purulent discharge → favours allergic rhinitis over sinusitis
questions.red: Periorbital swelling, visual change or severe headache with sinusitis → orbital or intracranial spread — emergency.

questions.ask: Any sore throat? Fever, or trouble opening your mouth?
questions.why: Most sore throat is viral pharyngitis; the job is to catch the bacterial minority and the rare deep-space emergency.
points: Acute sore throat + fever + tonsillar exudate → bacterial pharyngitis/tonsillitis (group A strep), or in adolescents, EBV
Unilateral severe pain + trismus + drooling → quinsy (peritonsillar abscess) — red flag
Sore throat + odynophagia + fever ± stridor → epiglottitis — red flag, do not examine the throat
questions.red: Trismus/drooling (quinsy) or stridor with sore throat (epiglottitis) are emergencies.

questions.ask: Any difficulty or pain swallowing?
