questions.why: Progressive dysphagia with weight loss is oesophageal/pharyngeal cancer until excluded — cross-reference the GI dysphagia entry for the solid-vs-liquid localisation.
points: Progressive dysphagia + weight loss → oesophageal/pharyngeal malignancy
Painful swallowing (odynophagia) → pharyngitis, tonsillitis, or rarely epiglottitis

questions.ask: Has your voice changed or become hoarse?
questions.why: Persistent hoarseness >3 weeks needs laryngoscopy — in a smoker it can be the first sign of laryngeal or lung cancer via recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement (cross-reference the Respiratory hoarseness entry).
points: Persistent hoarseness >3 weeks in a smoker → laryngeal or lung cancer until excluded
Hoarseness after a URTI, resolving within days–weeks → laryngitis — benign
questions.red: Persistent hoarseness >3 weeks needs laryngoscopy.

questions.ask: Any lumps or swelling in the neck?
questions.why: A persistent unilateral neck lump in an adult is malignancy until excluded — nodal, thyroid or salivary.
points: Persistent, unilateral, firm, in an adult → assume malignancy until excluded
Tender, bilateral, in a child or with a recent URTI → reactive lymphadenopathy
questions.red: Persistent unilateral neck lump in an adult → assume malignancy until excluded.

questions.ask: Any loss or blurring of vision — one eye or both, sudden or gradual? Any curtain or shadow?
questions.why: The tempo and pain split it into emergencies versus chronic causes.
points: Sudden painless monocular loss → retinal artery/vein occlusion, amaurosis fugax (TIA warning — cross-reference neuro), vitreous haemorrhage, retinal detachment (with flashes/floaters/curtain) — emergencies
Sudden loss + pain + headache/systemic → acute angle-closure glaucoma, optic neuritis, GCA (age >50, scalp/jaw symptoms)
Gradual painless → cataract, chronic glaucoma, macular degeneration, refractive/diabetic
questions.red: Sudden visual loss is an emergency — same-day ophthalmology.

questions.ask: Any redness or pain in the eye?
questions.why: The painful red eye is sight-threatening until proven otherwise; the benign mimic (conjunctivitis) is gritty and painless with normal vision.
points: Painful red eye + photophobia/reduced vision → sight-threatening: acute angle-closure glaucoma, uveitis, keratitis, scleritis
Red, gritty, discharge, vision normal, no pain → conjunctivitis — benign
questions.red: Painful red eye with reduced vision needs same-day ophthalmology.

questions.ask: Any double vision?
questions.why: Diplopia localises a cranial-nerve lesion (III, IV, VI) or raised ICP — cross-reference the Neurological special-senses entry.
points: → cranial nerve palsy: think microvascular, compressive (aneurysm — painful III with a fixed pupil is an emergency), or raised ICP

questions.ask: Any discharge from the eye?
questions.why: The character of the discharge separates the infective causes and flags when it's actually part of a sight-threatening picture rather than simple conjunctivitis.
points: Watery/mucopurulent, gritty, vision normal → conjunctivitis (viral or bacterial) — benign
Purulent discharge + pain + reduced vision → part of a sight-threatening picture, not simple conjunctivitis

items: Visual loss (sudden vs gradual, painful vs painless)

systems.drill: EARS: hearing loss (sudden? unilateral?), tinnitus, discharge, earache, vertigo · NOSE: blockage/discharge (unilateral = red flag), epistaxis, smell, facial pain · THROAT: sore throat, dysphagia, hoarseness >3 wks, neck lump · EYES: visual loss (sudden vs gradual, painful vs painless), red/painful eye, diplopia, discharge

systems.name: Reproductive & Sexual History
systems.scaffoldIntro: The reproductive history has one shared trunk and two sex-specific branches. Take the general sexual history first (it applies to everyone and sets the risk context), then branch:

chunks.gen: Activity, partners, contraception, pain, fertility, STI risk
LMP, cycle, bleeding, discharge, pregnancy, screening

systems.scaffoldOutro: **Framing matters here more than anywhere else.** Signpost why you're asking ("I ask everyone these questions, to make sure I don't miss anything"), use inclusive language, don't assume orientation or partners, and confirm confidentiality. The clinical red flags — ectopic pregnancy, testicular torsion, postmenopausal bleeding — sit inside an intensely personal history, so the manner of asking is part of the skill.

questions.ask: I'd like to ask some questions about your sexual health — I ask everyone these. Are you sexually active at the moment? Can you tell me about your partner(s)?
questions.why: Frames every reproductive symptom and sets the context for everything that follows. Ask sensitively, without assuming orientation, gender of partners, or number of partners.

questions.ask: What do you use for contraception, if anything? Do you use condoms?
questions.why: Contraceptive method affects the differential for abnormal bleeding and the discussion of STI risk — condom use specifically tracks STI/BBV exposure, separately from pregnancy prevention.

questions.ask: Any pain during sex?
questions.why: Deep dyspareunia points to a pelvic cause; superficial pain points to a local/vulval one — the distinction narrows the differential fast.
points: Deep dyspareunia + pelvic pain → endometriosis, PID

questions.ask: Are you currently trying to conceive, or have you had any difficulty with fertility?
questions.why: Fertility concerns reframe the relevance of menstrual, endocrine and structural findings, and often prompt the reason for presenting at all.

questions.ask: Any history of sexually transmitted infections, or contact with someone who has one? Any risk factors like injecting drug use or tattoos done outside a licensed studio?
questions.why: Sets pre-test probability for STI symptoms elsewhere in the screen and identifies who should be offered blood-borne virus testing.
points: BBV risk factors → offer testing (HIV, hepatitis B/C)

questions.ask: Any rashes, ulcers or lumps in the genital area?
questions.why: Character and pain of a genital ulcer is a fast bedside split between the common causes.
points: Discharge + dysuria + new partner → STI (chlamydia, gonorrhoea)
Genital ulcer — painful (herpes) vs painless (syphilis chancre)

questions.ask: When was your last period? Are your cycles regular? How heavy are they?
questions.why: The menstrual pattern is a vital sign of reproductive health.
points: Heavy regular periods → common cause of iron-deficiency anaemia
Secondary amenorrhoea → pregnancy first, then endocrine (thyroid, prolactin, PCOS)

questions.ask: Are your periods painful?
questions.why: Primary dysmenorrhoea (no pelvic pathology) is common and benign; pain that's new, progressive, or with deep dyspareunia and pelvic pain raises endometriosis.
points: Progressive, severe dysmenorrhoea + deep dyspareunia + pelvic pain → endometriosis

questions.ask: Any bleeding between periods, after sex, or after menopause?
questions.why: Bleeding outside the expected pattern is the single most important menstrual red-flag thread — each pattern points to a different structural cause.
points: Postmenopausal bleeding → endometrial cancer until excluded
Postcoital bleeding → cervical pathology (ectropion, cervicitis, cervical cancer) — check screening history
Intermenstrual bleeding → cervical or endometrial pathology — an indication for investigation (hysteroscopy ± endometrial biopsy)
questions.red: Postmenopausal bleeding is endometrial cancer until excluded.

questions.ask: Any pelvic pain or vaginal discharge?
questions.why: Discharge character and associated pain/fever separate the infective causes.
points: Discharge + pain + fever → PID; itchy discharge → candida (bacterial vaginosis is characteristically non-itchy — its clue is a thin grey, fishy-smelling discharge, not pruritus)

questions.ask: Is there any chance you could be pregnant? Tell me about any previous pregnancies.
questions.why: The possibility of pregnancy reframes any abdominal pain and must be established before imaging or prescribing.
points: Abdominal pain + missed period + possible pregnancy → ectopic pregnancy until excluded (a can't-miss)
Always establish pregnancy status before imaging or prescribing
questions.red: Abdominal pain + missed period → ectopic pregnancy until excluded.

questions.ask: Any milk discharge from the breasts, excess hair or acne, or menopausal symptoms?
questions.why: Links reproductive symptoms to the endocrine axes — each pattern points to a distinct hormonal cause.
points: Menopausal symptoms (hot flushes, mood swings, night sweats) → menopause

questions.ask: Are you up to date with cervical and breast screening?
questions.why: The two population cancer-screening programs — easy to skip if you're focused on the presenting symptom, but part of a complete reproductive history.

questions.ask: Any discharge from the penis, or rashes or ulcers?
questions.why: Urethral discharge is the cardinal STI symptom in men.

questions.ask: Any testicular pain, lumps or swelling?
questions.why: Testicular symptoms host two can't-miss diagnoses at opposite ends of the tempo spectrum — a painless lump and a painful acute scrotum.
points: Painless testicular lump → testicular cancer until excluded
questions.red: Sudden severe testicular pain in a young man → testicular torsion (surgical emergency).

questions.ask: Any difficulty with erections?
questions.why: Erectile dysfunction is an early vascular marker — it shares risk factors with IHD and often predates a cardiac event — and a common drug/endocrine effect.
points: ED + cardiovascular risk factors → endothelial/vascular disease; review antihypertensives, antidepressants, and mood

questions.ask: Any urinary symptoms, or have you discussed prostate checks?
questions.why: Prostate disease presents through the voiding LUTS screen (cross-reference GU) as much as through a screening conversation.
points: Prostate: voiding LUTS (cross-reference GU), family history, screening discussion

systems.drill: **GENERAL:** active?, partners (gender/number/type), contraception/condoms, dyspareunia, fertility, STI contact, BBV risk (IVDU/tattoos), genital lesions · **FEMALE:** LMP + cycle + volume, dysmenorrhoea, abnormal bleeding (postmenopausal/postcoital/intermenstrual), pelvic pain + discharge, pregnancy status + obstetric history, galactorrhoea/hyperandrogenism/menopause, cervical + breast screening · **MALE:** urethral discharge, testicular pain/lump, erectile function, prostate screening
systems.clnote: Signpost why you ask ("I ask everyone these"), use inclusive language, confirm confidentiality.

cases.stem: 58-year-old man with 30 minutes of central chest tightness radiating to the left arm, sweaty and nauseated.

options.q: Character, radiation & relation to exertion (SOCRATES)
options.why: Central, crushing, radiating to jaw/arm, exertional and relieved by rest/GTN points to ACS; tearing to the back would redirect you to dissection. This is the pivot of the whole assessment.

options.q: Is the pain sharp and worse on inspiration (pleuritic)?
options.why: A pleuritic quality pulls you toward PE, pericarditis or pneumothorax and away from ACS — a genuine discriminator worth one question.

options.q: Orthopnoea and PND
options.why: Screens for heart failure as context and for decompensation — useful background, though not the immediate rule-in for this acute presentation.

options.q: Cardiac risk factors (HTN, diabetes, lipids, smoking, family history)
options.why: These set the pre-test probability. The same pain in a diabetic smoker with a family history is a different problem — it changes how hard you rule ACS in.

options.q: Exertional syncope or presyncope
options.why: Points to aortic stenosis, HOCM or arrhythmia — a must-not-miss that changes disposition and warns of sudden death.

options.q: Change in bowel habit
options.why: No discriminating value for acute chest pain — this belongs to the GI/colorectal screen, not here.

options.q: Morning joint stiffness
options.why: Irrelevant to the acute chest-pain differential; a rheumatological screen question with no bearing on ACS.

options.q: Calf swelling or recent immobility
options.why: Feeds the PE branch of the differential — worth asking because PE is a can-miss cause of chest pain and breathlessness.

cases.stem: 67-year-old woman, gradually more breathless over months, now stops after 50 metres. Ex-smoker.

options.q: Orthopnoea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea
options.why: The single best bedside discriminator: positive answers pull you strongly toward left heart failure over lung disease as the cause of the dyspnoea.

options.q: Wheeze, cough and sputum
options.why: Pulls the differential the other way — toward COPD/asthma. Pairing this against the orthopnoea/PND answer is exactly how you separate cardiac from respiratory dyspnoea.

options.q: Ankle swelling, worse by evening
options.why: Bilateral pitting oedema with the congestion cluster supports heart failure; helps build the cardiac picture.

options.q: Smoking history in pack-years
options.why: Quantifies the dominant risk factor for both COPD and IHD — essential context that shifts pre-test probability for the whole differential.

options.q: Haemoptysis and weight loss
options.why: A must-ask in any older smoker with respiratory symptoms — screens for the lung cancer hiding behind "COPD".

options.q: Occupational exposures (asbestos, dusts)
options.why: Lifetime exposure history can reveal fibrosis or mesothelioma presenting decades later — a reasonable branch to explore.

options.q: Dysuria and frequency
options.why: A urinary screen question with no role in evaluating chronic breathlessness.

options.q: Skin rash distribution
options.why: No discriminating value for this presentation.

cases.stem: 24-year-old with a sudden, severe "worst headache of my life", peaking in seconds, now with neck stiffness.

options.q: Speed of onset — did it peak instantly (thunderclap)?
options.why: Instant, worst-ever, "hit on the head" onset is subarachnoid haemorrhage until excluded — the single most important question here.

options.q: Fever, neck stiffness and photophobia
options.why: The meningitis cluster — a must-not-miss infective emergency that overlaps this presentation.

options.q: Worse in the morning or on coughing/bending, with vomiting
options.why: Screens for raised intracranial pressure from a mass — a reasonable red-flag branch to cover.

options.q: Focal neurological deficit or altered consciousness
options.why: A neuro deficit or reduced consciousness reclassifies any headache as sinister and localises the problem — a must-not-miss (the N and S of SNOOP).

options.q: Previous similar headaches with aura, nausea, photophobia
options.why: Establishes whether this fits a prior migraine pattern — but a first thunderclap must never be attributed to migraine without exclusion.

options.q: Scalp tenderness and jaw claudication
options.why: These flag giant cell arteritis, a disease of the over-50s — low yield in a 24-year-old, though part of the general headache screen.

options.q: Bowel habit and PR bleeding
options.why: No relevance to an acute headache — belongs to the GI screen.

options.q: Ankle swelling
options.why: No discriminating value here.

cases.stem: 72-year-old man with 3 months of unintentional weight loss and fatigue.

options.q: Quantify the loss and confirm it is unintentional
options.why: Anchors the whole workup — >5% unintentional loss over 6–12 months is significant and separates true red-flag loss from dieting or fluid shifts.

options.q: Fever and drenching night sweats
options.why: Completes the B-symptom triad — pointing toward lymphoma, TB or other chronic infection/malignancy.

options.q: Change in bowel habit and rectal bleeding
options.why: Colorectal cancer is a leading cause of weight loss in this age group; iron-deficiency anaemia from a right-sided tumour also fits.

options.q: Appetite — increased or decreased?
options.why: Weight loss with a good appetite suggests a hypermetabolic cause (hyperthyroid, diabetes); with poor appetite, malignancy/depression — a neat fork.

options.q: Lymphadenopathy and generalised itch
options.why: Screens the lymphoreticular causes; painless rubbery nodes with itch point to lymphoma.

options.q: Heat intolerance, tremor, palpitations
options.why: Screens for hyperthyroidism — a treatable cause of weight loss despite a good appetite.

options.q: Mood, anhedonia and sleep
options.why: Depression is a common and reversible cause of weight loss in the elderly and is easily missed if not asked about.

options.q: Morning joint stiffness
options.why: Low yield for undifferentiated weight loss.

cases.stem: 55-year-old with an episode of transient loss of consciousness while running.

options.q: Was it during exertion?
options.why: Exertional syncope points to aortic stenosis, HOCM or ventricular arrhythmia — the dangerous causes that carry a risk of sudden death. This reframes everything.

options.q: Any warning or prodrome (nausea, greying vision, sweating)?
options.why: A prodrome triggered by standing/pain suggests benign vasovagal syncope; no warning suggests an arrhythmic (cardiac) cause — a core discriminator.

options.q: Collateral history from a witness
options.why: The patient by definition did not see the event — a witness account of jerking, colour, duration and recovery often makes the diagnosis.

options.q: Tongue-biting (lateral), post-ictal confusion/drowsiness
options.why: Separates a seizure from syncope — a different system, different management. (Jerk duration is unreliable; the lateral tongue-bite and post-ictal state are the real discriminators.)

options.q: Family history of sudden cardiac death
options.why: Flags inherited channelopathies and HOCM — a must-ask that changes risk and investigation.

options.q: Palpitations before or after the event
options.why: Points toward a primary arrhythmia as the mechanism.

options.q: Dysuria and frequency
options.why: No role in evaluating a blackout.

options.q: Skin rash
options.why: No discriminating value here.

cases.stem: 40-year-old with a single acutely hot, swollen, exquisitely painful big toe overnight.

options.q: Fever and systemic upset
options.why: A single acutely hot joint is septic arthritis until proven otherwise — fever and systemic upset raise that must-not-miss diagnosis, which needs aspiration not reassurance.

options.q: Speed of onset and prior similar attacks
options.why: Rapid overnight onset in the first MTP with prior self-limiting attacks is the classic gout story — but it never excludes sepsis on its own.

options.q: Alcohol intake, diet and diuretic use
options.why: Precipitants of gout — useful for the crystal-arthropathy branch and for management.

options.q: Recent trauma or skin break near the joint
options.why: A portal of entry raises the probability of septic arthritis — a relevant discriminator.

options.q: Morning stiffness duration and other joints involved
options.why: A polyarticular symmetrical pattern with prolonged stiffness would redirect you toward inflammatory arthritis rather than a monoarthritis.

options.q: Psoriasis, nail changes, eye or bowel symptoms
options.why: Screens the seronegative spondyloarthropathies as an alternative cause of the arthritis.

options.q: Cough and sputum
options.why: No bearing on an acute monoarthritis.

options.q: Visual changes
options.why: Low yield for this presentation.

cases.stem: 30-year-old woman, 6 weeks of low mood and loss of interest, presenting reluctantly.

options.q: Suicidal thoughts, plan, means and intent
options.why: The most important question in the encounter. Asking is protective, not suggestive — a plan with means and intent marks high acute risk and cannot be deferred.

options.q: Anhedonia and the SIGECAPS cluster
options.why: Low mood plus anhedonia are the two core criteria; SIGECAPS establishes whether the threshold for major depression is met and gauges severity.

options.q: Ever had a period of elevated mood, reduced need for sleep, risk-taking?
options.why: Screening for bipolarity is essential before treatment — antidepressants can precipitate mania if a manic history is missed.

options.q: Alcohol and recreational drug use
options.why: Substances cause, mimic and complicate depression — an important comorbidity and modifiable factor.

options.q: Cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, fatigue
options.why: Screens for hypothyroidism, a classic organic mimic of depression that is easily reversed if found.

options.q: Recent psychosocial stressors and supports
options.why: Distinguishes an adjustment reaction from major depression and identifies protective factors relevant to risk.

options.q: Change in bowel habit with blood
options.why: No discriminating value for this presentation.

options.q: Joint swelling
options.why: Low yield here.

cases.stem: 19-year-old, 3 weeks of thirst, passing large volumes of urine, and 4 kg weight loss.

options.q: Polyuria, polydipsia, nocturia and blurred vision
options.why: The osmotic symptom cluster is the classic presentation of hyperglycaemia — confirming it makes new diabetes the leading diagnosis.

options.q: Abdominal pain, vomiting, deep or rapid breathing
options.why: These flag diabetic ketoacidosis — the must-not-miss emergency in new type 1 diabetes. A young, rapidly-losing-weight patient is exactly the at-risk group.

options.q: Weight change and appetite
options.why: Weight loss despite a normal or increased appetite is the hypermetabolic signature of insulin deficiency — a core discriminator here.

options.q: Recurrent thrush, skin or urinary infections and slow healing
options.why: The quieter hyperglycaemia clues — they add supporting evidence and hint at duration.

options.q: Family history of diabetes or autoimmune disease
options.why: Sets pre-test probability and hints at type 1 (autoimmune) versus type 2.

options.q: Tremor, sweating and confusion relieved by eating
options.why: These are hypoglycaemia symptoms — not relevant before any glucose-lowering treatment has started, so low yield at first presentation.

options.q: Heat intolerance and palpitations
options.why: A reasonable branch — hyperthyroidism overlaps via weight loss despite a good appetite (the polyuria here is osmotic, not thyroid), so it is worth one discriminating question.

options.q: Snoring and daytime sleepiness
options.why: No discriminating value for this osmotic presentation.

cases.stem: 34-year-old woman, 3 months of weight loss despite eating more, palpitations, tremor and feeling hot all the time.

options.q: Heat intolerance, sweating and fine tremor
options.why: The hyperthyroid metabolic signature — with weight loss despite a good appetite, this cluster makes thyrotoxicosis the leading diagnosis.

options.q: Palpitations — rate and regularity (tap it out)
options.why: Thyrotoxicosis commonly causes AF; characterising the palpitations both supports the diagnosis and screens for its dangerous complication.

options.q: Neck swelling and obstructive symptoms (SOB, stridor, dysphagia)
options.why: Screens for a goitre and, importantly, compressive complications — a relevant branch in any thyroid presentation.

options.q: Eye changes — grittiness, prominence, double vision
options.why: Points specifically to Graves’ ophthalmopathy, which would identify the cause of the thyrotoxicosis.

options.q: Bowel habit — diarrhoea or constipation
options.why: Diarrhoea fits the hypermetabolic picture; asking helps confirm the systemic pattern.

options.q: Anxiety, restlessness and heat — or the mirror: cold, low mood, constipation
options.why: Anchoring against the hypothyroid mirror sharpens the pattern recognition and catches an atypical presentation.

options.q: Suicidal ideation
options.why: Not indicated by this presentation — thyrotoxicosis can cause anxiety, but there is no depressive picture here to warrant a risk assessment as a screening question.

options.q: Intermittent claudication
options.why: No discriminating value for a thyrotoxic presentation.

cases.stem: 26-year-old woman with lower abdominal pain and light vaginal bleeding; her period is 2 weeks late.

options.q: Could you be pregnant? Last menstrual period and cycle
options.why: Abdominal pain plus a missed period is an ectopic pregnancy until excluded — a can’t-miss, potentially life-threatening diagnosis. Establishing pregnancy status is the first move.

options.q: Character and site of the pain (SOCRATES)
options.why: Unilateral pelvic pain with shoulder-tip pain or syncope raises a ruptured ectopic; characterising it drives urgency and the differential.

options.q: Sexual history, contraception and STI risk
options.why: Contraceptive method affects ectopic risk (e.g. IUD, progestogen-only), and PID is a leading alternative cause of pelvic pain — both need the sexual history.

options.q: Vaginal discharge and fever
options.why: Discharge with fever points toward pelvic inflammatory disease as the alternative diagnosis.

options.q: Dizziness, fainting or shoulder-tip pain
options.why: These suggest intra-abdominal bleeding from a ruptured ectopic — a haemodynamic red flag that escalates the situation immediately.

options.q: Obstetric history (previous pregnancies, ectopics, terminations)
options.why: A previous ectopic or pelvic surgery raises the risk of another — useful for weighting the differential.

options.q: Dysuria and urinary frequency
options.why: A UTI can cause lower abdominal pain and is worth excluding, though it does not address the pregnancy question.

options.q: Morning joint stiffness
options.why: No discriminating value for acute pelvic pain.

cases.stem: 64-year-old man with several months of food sticking in the lower chest — first with meat and bread, now even fluids won't go down — and a loose waistband; 40-pack-year smoker, drinks daily.

options.q: Do you struggle with solids only, or with liquids too — and which came first?
options.why: The central discriminator: solids-first progressing to liquids is the signature of a mechanical obstruction (stricture or carcinoma), whereas solids-and-liquids equally from the outset points to a motility disorder like achalasia. This history — solids then liquids — is textbook mechanical.

options.q: Has it been getting steadily worse over weeks to months, or does it come and go?
options.why: Relentlessly progressive dysphagia is an alarm feature demanding urgent endoscopy — it suggests a stricture or oesophageal carcinoma. Intermittent, non-progressive dysphagia would instead suggest an oesophageal ring or eosinophilic oesophagitis.

options.q: Have you lost weight without trying, and how much over what time?
options.why: Unintentional weight loss alongside dysphagia is a red-flag combination for oesophageal malignancy (Talley lists dysphagia, weight loss and bleeding as the core alarm triad). Quantifying it sizes the concern and drives the urgency of investigation.

options.q: Can you point to where the food seems to hold up or stick?
options.why: Localising the hold-up helps anatomically: pointing to the lower retrosternal area fits a distal mechanical obstruction, which matches this presentation. Higher obstructions may be felt anywhere retrosternally, so it narrows but doesn't clinch.

options.q: Do you have long-standing heartburn or acid coming up into your throat?
options.why: A history of reflux raises the possibility of a peptic stricture or Barrett's oesophagus with malignant change — relevant context for the cause of the narrowing. Its presence points toward GORD-related disease as the mechanism.

options.q: Do you cough, choke, or get fluid coming down your nose when you start to swallow?
options.why: These features flag oropharyngeal dysphagia from a neuromuscular cause (e.g. bulbar palsy), a different problem from oesophageal obstruction. Their absence here helps confirm the block is oesophageal rather than in the pharynx.

options.q: Do you have asthma or hay fever?
options.why: Atopy would support eosinophilic oesophagitis, but that typically causes intermittent dysphagia and food-bolus impaction in younger patients — a poor fit for this older smoker with progressive solids-to-liquids dysphagia and weight loss. Low yield here.

options.q: Have you had any burning or frequency when passing urine?
options.why: A urinary screening question from an unrelated system with no bearing on swallowing difficulty — a plausible-sounding distractor that adds nothing to this oesophageal presentation.

cases.stem: 68-year-old man with a single episode of painless visible (macroscopic) blood in the urine; long smoking history, otherwise well.

options.q: Was it painful or completely painless — any stinging on passing urine, or loin-to-groin pain?
options.why: Painless visible haematuria in an older smoker is urological malignancy (bladder/renal) until excluded; dysuria would point to UTI and severe loin-to-groin colic to a stone, so this one answer reshapes the whole differential.

options.q: Were there clots, and was the blood at the start, the end, or right through the stream?
options.why: Clots indicate the bleeding is non-glomerular (favouring a urological source such as tumour), and blood throughout the stream localises above the bladder neck, whereas initial or terminal bleeding suggests a urethral or prostatic origin.

options.q: How much have you smoked over your life, and any work with industrial dyes, rubber or chemicals?
options.why: Smoking is the dominant risk factor for urothelial (bladder) cancer and occupational aromatic-amine exposure (dyes, rubber, chemicals) is the classic second one — in this long-term smoker both sharply raise the pre-test probability of malignancy.

options.q: Any trouble starting, a weak stream, dribbling or a sense of not emptying?
options.why: Voiding/obstructive LUTS are common at 68 and point to the prostate (BPH, or cancer), a plausible co-existing source of bleeding — but they never let you drop the malignancy workup that painless haematuria demands.

options.q: Is the urine frothy, and have you had a recent sore throat or new ankle swelling?
options.why: Frothy urine (proteinuria), synpharyngitic haematuria after a sore throat (IgA nephropathy) or oedema would redirect you toward a glomerular cause, distinguishing a renal-medical picture from the surgical/urological one this presentation otherwise suggests.

options.q: Any unintended weight loss, poor appetite, or new bone pain?
options.why: Constitutional loss plus bone pain would signal advanced or metastatic urological cancer — the must-not-miss escalation of painless haematuria in a smoker, changing urgency and disposition.

options.q: Any heartburn or acid reflux after meals?
options.why: A gastrointestinal screening question with no bearing on the source of visible haematuria — it belongs to a different system and adds no discriminating value here.

options.q: Do you get morning stiffness in the hands lasting over an hour?
options.why: An inflammatory-arthritis screen that is irrelevant to this urological presentation and does nothing to separate the causes of blood in the urine.

cases.stem: 30-year-old with a few weeks of bruises appearing without knocks, bleeding gums when brushing, mounting fatigue, and one sore throat after another that just won't clear.

options.q: Are you also getting infections you can't shake and feeling breathless or exhausted, all around the same time as the bruising?
options.why: Bleeding, infection and fatigue arriving together means all three cell lines are failing at once — the pancytopenia of marrow failure or acute leukaemia, the must-not-miss diagnosis here demanding an urgent full blood count and film.

options.q: Where does the bleeding happen — pinhead spots and bruises in the skin, gums and nose, or deep into joints and muscles?
options.why: Mucocutaneous bleeding — petechiae, purpura, gum and nose bleeding — points to a platelet problem (thrombocytopenia), which fits this picture and separates it from the deep joint/muscle bleeding of a coagulation-factor disorder.

options.q: Have you had drenching night sweats, unexplained weight loss, fevers, or noticed any lumps in your neck, armpits or groin?
options.why: B-symptoms and lymphadenopathy would signal leukaemia or lymphoma infiltrating the marrow — directly relevant, since these are exactly the constitutional clues that accompany a haematological malignancy causing this bleeding.

options.q: How severe and how frequent are these infections — needing antibiotics, or landing you in bed?
options.why: Grading the recurrent sore throats and infections gauges how depressed the neutrophils are; severe or recurrent infection is a warning sign of underlying marrow disease worth characterising in this patient.

options.q: Are you taking any blood-thinning or anti-inflammatory tablets — warfarin, a DOAC, aspirin, clopidogrel — or started any new medication recently?
options.why: Anticoagulants and antiplatelets are the commonest everyday cause of easy bruising and bleeding, and some drugs suppress the marrow — a simple, correctable explanation that must be excluded before chasing rarer diagnoses.

options.q: Does anyone in your family have a bleeding disorder, or bruise and bleed easily like this?
options.why: A family history would raise inherited bleeding disorders such as von Willebrand disease or haemophilia; its absence in a young adult with new-onset bleeding pushes you toward an acquired marrow or platelet cause.

options.q: Do you get heartburn or acid reflux after meals?
options.why: A gastro-oesophageal screening question from an unrelated system with no bearing on bruising or bleeding — a plausible-sounding distractor that adds nothing to this haematological presentation.

options.q: Do you have a long-standing cough or wheeze?
options.why: A respiratory screen question that doesn't discriminate here; chronic cough and wheeze have no place in the workup of easy bruising and marrow failure in this patient.

cases.stem: 45-year-old fair-skinned landscaper noticing a mole on his back that has grown over the past few months, with a ragged edge and patches of darker and lighter brown; years of outdoor work and several blistering childhood sunburns.

options.q: Has the mole changed — grown larger, changed shape or colour, and over what time?
options.why: Change (evolution) is the single most important melanoma alarm and the 'E' of ABCDE — a pigmented lesion that is enlarging, altering shape or shifting colour over weeks to months is suspicious until proven otherwise. This history of recent growth and new colour variation is the pivot of the whole assessment and mandates excision biopsy.

options.q: Is it asymmetrical, with an irregular border, more than one colour, or wider than about 6 mm?
options.why: The ABCD morphology (Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Colour variegation, Diameter >6 mm) separates a benign naevus from melanoma — this lesion's ragged edge and mixed brown shades tick several boxes and raise the pre-test probability sharply. In Australia, the highest-incidence melanoma country, a low threshold for these features saves lives.

options.q: Has the mole bled, become itchy, crusted or ulcerated?
options.why: Bleeding, itch, crusting or ulceration in a pigmented lesion are late red-flag signs of an evolving or thickening melanoma and warn of a worse prognosis. Their presence would add urgency to an already suspicious lesion in this vignette.

options.q: Have you felt any lumps in the armpits, neck or groin, or had unexplained weight loss or fatigue?
options.why: Regional lymphadenopathy and constitutional symptoms screen for spread of melanoma to draining nodes or beyond — a must-not-miss that changes staging and disposition. Talley stresses examining the regional lymphatic field whenever a neoplastic skin lesion is suspected.

options.q: How much sun exposure have you had, and did you have blistering sunburns as a child?
options.why: Cumulative sun exposure and a history of blistering sunburn are established melanoma risk factors that raise this outdoor worker's baseline risk — sound Australian context that supports concern but does not by itself diagnose the lesion.

options.q: Do you burn easily and tan poorly, and have you ever had a skin cancer or a family member with melanoma?
options.why: Fair skin that burns rather than tans (Fitzpatrick type I–II), a personal history of skin cancer and a family history of melanoma all compound risk, and this fair-skinned man fits the high-risk phenotype. Useful for stratifying risk, though the lesion's own features drive the decision to biopsy.

options.q: Have you changed your soap, shampoo or washing powder recently?
options.why: A contact-dermatitis screening question that is relevant to an itchy rash but adds nothing to the assessment of a solitary changing pigmented mole — a plausible dermatology-flavoured distractor with no bearing on melanoma.

options.q: Have you noticed any change in your bowel habit?
options.why: A gastrointestinal screening question from an unrelated system with no discriminating value for a pigmented skin lesion — it belongs to the GI review, not here.

cases.stem: 52-year-old who over a single day developed muffled hearing in the right ear with a feeling of fullness and ringing in that ear; no preceding cold, and no ear pain or discharge.

options.q: Did this come on suddenly over hours to a day, or has it built up gradually over weeks to months?
options.why: Hearing loss developing over hours to three days is the defining feature of an otological emergency, whereas a gradual course over months points instead to presbyacusis or a slowly enlarging lesion — pinning down this one-day onset is the pivot of the whole assessment.

options.q: Is there any ear pain, discharge, wax or blockage, or did it follow a cold?
options.why: With no pain, discharge, wax or preceding URTI, a conductive cause (wax, middle-ear effusion, perforation) is unlikely, leaving sudden sensorineural hearing loss — an otological emergency needing same-day ENT referral within the treatable (steroid) window.

options.q: Do you have any spinning or dizziness (vertigo) with the hearing loss?
options.why: Vertigo localises the problem to the inner ear and screens for Ménière's disease (the classic triad of fluctuating sensorineural loss, tinnitus and vertigo); its presence or absence materially shifts the differential for this sudden unilateral loss.

options.q: Any facial weakness, limb weakness, slurred speech, double vision or severe unsteadiness?
options.why: These flag a central cause — a brainstem or AICA-territory stroke can present as sudden unilateral hearing loss — a must-not-miss that needs urgent imaging rather than ENT referral alone.

options.q: Are the hearing loss and ringing confined to the one ear, and have they persisted?
options.why: Persistent unilateral sensorineural loss with unilateral tinnitus should prompt exclusion of an acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma), so confirming the symptoms are one-sided and ongoing guides later imaging.

options.q: Any recent loud noise exposure, or medicines such as gentamicin, cisplatin, water tablets or high-dose aspirin?
options.why: Loud-noise exposure and ototoxic drugs (aminoglycosides, cisplatin, loop diuretics, salicylates) are recognised causes of sensorineural loss worth excluding, though they less often produce this abrupt, strictly unilateral pattern.

options.q: Have you noticed any change in your bowel habit or blood in your stool?
options.why: Bowel habit belongs to the colorectal screen and has no bearing on sudden unilateral hearing loss — a distractor from an unrelated system.

options.q: Do you get seasonal sneezing with an itchy, blocked nose?
options.why: Allergic rhinitis can cause bilateral Eustachian-tube fullness but not an abrupt one-sided sensorineural loss with tinnitus — a plausible-sounding but low-yield line for this presentation.
